GOVERNMENT POSITION ON CANADA-WIDE HOME INSULATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In view of the steps the Carter administration is taking to conserve energy in the United States and in view of Canada's dwindling proven oil reserves, which for the past seven years have declined each year from the previous year's level, is the government prepared to consider a Canadawide home insulation program which, according to a government study, would reduce residential heating costs by 37 per cent, save this country $1.25 billion annually and reduce our oil import deficit by $750 million per year? Is the government giving consideration to such a program?

speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, we are giving consideration to that. That was discussed by the provincial ministers during the recent federal-provincial energy ministers' conference. subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON CANADA-WIDE HOME INSULATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that a Canada-wide program would give to each householder a $400 grant and a $600 loan-the loan being repaid out of the $180 a year which each family would save, and at 8 per cent interest it could be paid off in four years-in view of the fact that for $300 million a year the government could provide for the insulation of every home in Canada in ten years or with $600 million a year could provide for the insulation of every home in Canada in five years, and in view of the fact that by 1985 our deficit on oil imports will amount to between $4 billion and $5 billion, does the government not think it is good business to institute the kind of program I have just outlined?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON CANADA-WIDE HOME INSULATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, quite obviously we do think home insulation is a very good kind of program. That is the reason we introduced the first two programs in North America, in Prince Edward Island and in Nova Scotia. In Nova Scotia there is a grant program and a loan program, and there is a grant program in Prince Edward Island. We believe that home re-insulation makes sense for the homeowner, for the provinces and, in the broader sense, for the people of Canada. As I have said on many occasions we have endorsed home insulation programs, and we encourage other provinces to follow the lead of the province of British Columbia, which is providing loans through its public utilities commission for homeowners.

speechtext:

speechtext:
Order, please. The point at issue is that the Prime Minister of this country, or of any country, has many responsibilities. According to the definition that has been placed on the ambit of the question period, questions must be addressed to ministers of the Crown in respect of their administrative responsibilities. The question to be decided by the Chair is not whether the question asked relates to any of the several responsibilities of the Prime Minister, or any other minister, but whether it relates to his administrative responsibilities.
It seems to me that the question directed to the Prime Minister relates, perhaps, to the responsibility which any political leader might have in respect to setting, as the hon. member for Annapolis Valley has just described it, a moral tone or political philosophy before the nation. That does not relate to his administrative responsibilities on which questions ought to be permitted in the question period. That is the
(Mr. LcBlanc (Westmorland-Kcnt).]
difference. The hon. member may have occasion to put his question elsewhere. The question the Chair must decide is whether it is proper to put that question in the question period. If it does not touch on administrative competence, it is not a question the Prime Minister can or should answer.
It is a question of whether the question asked was in order. I find that the question was not in order within those terms.

The press has suggested that the Minister of Transport will not be in that position. Mr. Speaker, during the oral question period I asked the Prime Minister if, in the course of the negotiations which the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) had with the government and the federal Liberal party leaders, reference was made to the Canadian policy on bilingualism advocated by the Prime Minister since 1968. Will he or will he not make a statement in the House in the near future? Mr. Speaker, I can understand that the appointment of this minister has some significance in the west but it has an entirely different one for us in the province of Quebec.
Quebecers are struggling to have the French language respected and the right to speak French, and since 1968 they have heard the Liberal party talk about respect for language and equal opportunity. But today, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister brings within his cabinet an hon. member who, with all due respect, has always fiercely opposed the promotion of bilingualism in Quebec and elsewhere in Canada, who even said that he would forever refuse to learn a single word of French.
Mr. Speaker, this is a substantial issue. One wonders whether the hon. member for Crowfoot, out of ministerial solidarity, committed himself with the government to support openly the language policy of the government, whether the government simply rejected the importance of that policy in the west, or whether it is merely vote-catching maneuvers.
That issue, for us in Quebec, is fundamental. My question of privilege bears on the following point:
In view of the premises of the Prime Minister, he told me in his reply to direct my question to the minister, which meant that the latter would be in position to reply to me today; however, you did not allow this minister to reply to me; as a

I think, Mr. Speaker, that this is an important matter. Order, please. The hon. member for Bellechasse has raised a further argument with respect to the same question raised by his leader, and I have ruled, I think, properly. In keeping with our past practices, the propriety of questions put to individual ministers, from a procedural point of view, is not decided by the Prime Minister. It is decided by the Chair. If the Prime Minister indicates that a certain question should be put to a particular minister, it still remains for the Chair in all circumstances to decide whether that question is put properly or not put properly to that minister.
The decision of the Chair with respect to a question on bilingual policy put to the new Minister without Portfolio would be precisely the same as if another hon. member asked a question as to whether the Minister of Transport supports the policy of the government in respect of regional development, whether the Minister of Finance supports the policy of the Minister of Labour, or whether the Minister of Labour supports the policy of the Minister of National Revenue.
Those questions are not proper and never have been, and in my opinion, they do not become proper simply because the House wants to find out if a new minister has policies which are consistent with those of his new leader. Those questions are very important; there is no question about that. There is no difficulty at all in understanding the desire of the House to have a commitment from a new minister with respect to such fundamental and important questions, but from a procedural point of view that is not the problem. The question is, what should be the scope of questions put to individual ministers in this House?
The practice has always been that they must fall within the individual administrative competence or responsibility of particular ministers, and in that respect it does not fall within the individual administrative competence of the new Minister without Portfolio to make pronouncements on the government's policy on bilingualism. I am sure the question will be asked again and again on occasions when the minister appears in public or anywhere else where questions might be put to him, and they might also be put to the Prime Minister as to whether he has received the minister's agreement.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my rising today springs from the answer given by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration when responding to a question regarding unemployment insurance payments to the 18,000 persons over 65 and under 70 and those people who were on dependency allowance benefits when the new act came into being in January, 1976. Today we were told quite emphatically by the minister that, in effect, we must pass Bill C-27, which includes an amendment.
We have raised this matter before, as you know, Mr. Speaker, and in the past we were told that the Department of Justice said no amendment was needed. Then the minister told us an amendment was needed. In committee we were told no amendment was needed and that the claims could be processed and benefits sent out to the claimants. When we raised a question of privilege in this House we were told that we needed an amendment, that the Department of Justice had given the wrong information to the minister and to his department and that all he had done was pass on the information. Yesterday afternoon when we were in committee we were told by the minister that he was looking for ways to get around this so-called amendment and to bring something before the House so that people could receive the benefits due to them.
When ministers give answers in the House and in committee, I put trust in those answers because this House is built on trust. When ministers give answers we make decisions in terms of our constituents and the areas we represent on the basis of those answers. So there has to be basic honesty and trust operating here.
The point I raise is that it is regrettable that we have a minister who has shilly-shallied and dilly-dallied and in effect has held to ransom 18,000 Canadians. It comes through very clearly every day we question him that he is saying to us, "If you pass Bill C-27, these people will get their payments". It is public knowledge that there are clauses in Bill C-27 with which members from Atlantic Canada on both the government side and the opposition side have great difficulty. The minister knows that very clearly, and it is obvious to all who want to observe the fact that the minister is holding 18,000 Canadians to ransom. I find that most regrettable.
The minister must operate on trust in the House. If he told us he is looking for an avenue to get around the impasse, we would be able to accept that, but when he puts the condition to us that we must pass Bill C-27, it indicates incompetence on
Business of the House
his part in the way he has handled this whole matter, and he should resign from his position.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a very simple point to raise with the President of the Privy Council. He has indicated his intention, if events follow along as he would like, to introduce a bill dealing with tax conventions. An essential feature of such bills is to contain a clause based upon what the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs has persuaded the House to accept with regard to any changes in the regulations being subject to affirmation or otherwise by the House by way of resolution.
When the former minister of justice, Mr. Turner, piloted through the House the statutory instruments legislation, there was an undertaking that the House would then move to adapt its rules to conform with the detailed procedures contained in that act. This was five years ago, and nothing has been done. In the interval we have passed four or five acts, and I am sure we will be asked to pass further acts as a result of the minister's intention with regard to dealing with affirmative and negative resolutions.
If the minister, as director of the business of the government is afraid of sending something to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, will he please lay down a direction in this respect? I say, on behalf of my colleagues, that there will be no further debate and that the motion to refer the question of affirmative and negative resolutions in so far as they apply to the rules of the House shall be considered by the committee, brought back and established according to the intention of the government with regard to legislation in the past.
We want this as much as the government, but for some reason there has been an inordinate reluctance to bring forward this item. We have had to dredge it out of the legislation and spell it out in lengthy amendments every time we have had a bill. Frankly, it is nonsense. Both sides of the House are agreed on the procedure that should be followed with regard to affirmative and negative resolutions.
At the time the minister brings forward a bill with regard to a tax convention, regardless of the merits of that particular

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned yesterday, I was just about to get to the main thrust of my speech after a short introduction.
First, I shall talk about agriculture and especially the latest dairy policy. In addition to the bill of $477 million that will be paid, Mr. Speaker, a principle of justice and equity will be

The Budget-Mr. Tessier
consecrated, and this is the merit of the 1977-78 dairy policy, that is that the poorer and less favoured in the system have now a means to protect themselves against the justice of the strong. And curiously enough, this fight that we have waged is a typical and also an illustration of the instruments of power in the House of Commons. Indeed, to do a good job as a member of parliament we must not only face the public service, but also win over it. Of course, the dairy policy includes elements which will be difficult to apply since there are many variables and virtually every producer has become a special case. However, the adjustments are essential and necessary and they are an integral part of the dairy policy. Beyond these adjustments, there are fights which are nearly institutionalized and which are damaging since they do not do anything to the producers themselves and tend to destroy the government. This last year has given important evidence of this. The producers have been used by certain manipulators. The rules of the games have been distorted either by personal interests or by conflicts of interest. When you add to all this the power, the dominating public servants, we can have the same type of situation as that which we witnessed during the milk crisis in 1976-77, because for the public service, the only rule that seems to apply is always to win as and when it wants to, whatever the price.
I would like to note that the results obtained at the announcement of the latest dairy policy were simply those expected more than a year ago, and I am still convinced that today's offer is reasonable without offering the minimum. However, it is far from the maximum mentioned by certain members, who act as the champions of the public service or the consumers.
I would not like to be unduly rash but I want to warn our opponents that if we deal with working conditions and remuneration, farmers will have a field day of it for many years to come. But if w.e place the milk issue in the narrower context of national unity or, to be more specific, the obscure corridor of profitable federalism, we have a situation like the one prevailing in Quebec where the government floundered or was "hoodwinked" all the way. The question is, who is to blame?
It is simply coincidence that Quebec happens to produce mainly industrial milk while Ontario produces fluid milk for the most part? Is it pure chance that Quebec has two milk producer federations, of which, the smaller appears to be the stronger, labour wise, while the federation of industrial milk producers, although six times as large, seems to be the weaker? Is it only by chance that Ontario has only one such federation strongly dominated by fluid milk producers? Is it a coincidence that the marketing board plays second fiddle to fluid milk producers? Who controls the Canadian Federation of milk producers? Who controls the Canadian Agriculture Federation? Who controlled and still does the Quebec Agricultural Producers' Union? What is the Department of Agriculture's stand with regards to the milk industry? How could it accept the iniquity and unfairness of the 1975-76 policy?

This policy cost industrial milk producers about $58 million, while industrial milk producers in Quebec had to pay out $34 million. Who could dispute that? Indeed, the quota system cost industrial milk producers some $30 million. The levy cost them $18,401,429. Industrial milk producers also had to pay out $9,570,260 in subsidies for a grand total of $57,971,689.
Such is the argument of those who claim that the industrial milk industry was being taken down by the fluid milk producers. But when Separatists got hold of this argument in Quebec, they accused the Federal government of stealing $35 million from them. No one has the right to rob Quebec, just as we do not have the right to let producers cheat one another. The Cabinet has understood this and so should the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis).
We will keep fighting as we know that we have a just cause. We can only hope that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) will find the means to help the other categories of producers in order to ensure for each of them a fair return for their work. Mr. Speaker, besides the problem of agriculture, there is another area in the 1977-78 budget which is of great concern to me, and that is industrial decentralization. And believe me, I am not seeking a theoretical definition but a declaration to the effect that industrial decentralization must be extended to our rural areas, as there are many regions where agriculture alone cannot generate a healthy and dynamic economy.
At the moment, the government does not have the appropriate means to deal with this and we shall have to find other ways, since it is our contention that the government is responsible not only for unemployment insurance but also and above all for work insurance and will always be. There is no point in reminding the House of the failure of the Regional Economic Expansion Department in its fight against regional disparities since it was on the whole a success, but now we need another instrument, to develop and secure the means to provide our rural areas with a prosperous economy which our people greatly need, not just to make ends meet but to live comfortably and grow.
In Quebec especially we have been hearing phrases such as: Let civil servants serve! Let students study! Let teachers teach! Let nurses nurse! Let workers work! But we have yet to hear: Let the unemployed remain unemployed! But unless there is a change it will be said and who will be responsible? If the government wants to avoid that, it must say right now: Let "industries produce"!
Let me refer for a moment to my experience as mayor of the municipality of Lake Megantic. Why should anyone with a little money send it down the drain, in the almost chaotic situation we now face, in an attempt to create jobs? Because the next day he is sure of nothing. Businessmen told me, and rightly so in my view: "We are ready to produce, we are even ready to work day and night, seven days a week if need be, because this is our job.
April 21, 1977

But one thing we are not ready to do, is build walls and roofs when there is a risk of not having workers to do the work, or work to give workers." The answer to that is: Let the government build walls and roofs for workers to work under, and let industries produce. Such is the way to induce and direct industrial decentralization and to give work to those who can and want to work.
Let me have $5 million for my constituency. More than 1,500 permanent jobs will be created and anyone will be able to see that such an initiative will be profitable to all Canadians. In this way, a sense of purpose will not only be restored but become accessible, and this is something we have all been waiting for. Thirdly, when reference is made to inflation, the spiralling wage increases, the productivity gap, even when such reference comes from the Minister of Finance, I wonder if anybody is listening. As for us, if we consider the matter more thoroughly, we become alarmist, especially in non-industrial-ized areas with low population, because it means an exodus or poverty but just the same, individually or as a whole, we are responsible.
Mr. Speaker, an assembly such as ours must face those facts daily but unfortunately they are not known outside the House as they should be. What is our responsibility in that regard? As a member, as a government or as a Parliament? Should we become salesmen? Mr. Speaker, the fact is that as long as we are here, we try to offer more than we can afford since our constituents can no longer pay. What should we do then? Let us reconsider together a new order for a new balance in Canada and afterwards let us sell it to our constituents.since the procedure is out-of-date and too many cannot make use of their aptitudes or their devotion. Energies and skills are wasted. The very credibility of Parliament is at stake, and the credulousness of our constituents is not to be taken advantage of any longer.
In summary, the budget speech is a perfect demonstration that members of parliament are no longer what they ought to be, for the only thing they can do is to ask, while Parliament has nothing left to give and they have the individual and collective obligation to refuse. Let us stop slighting our respective constituencies, for the times we are now living in are not for speeches, but for necessary action.
I remain convinced that I am more useful to my constituents at home and when they need me than when I try to have them believe that I can do something for them here in the House. They are honest with me, I need them to continue to be so and that is why I want to be honest with them.
We have therefore the duty to advise the public of the limits within which we operate. In this endeavour, we must try and do a good job. By way of a conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that if a budget did not hurt, it would not be a real budget. Of course, we are aware of a great many needs, and all of us are eager to find the way to meet these needs effectively; unfortunately we could not do it without writing a cheque, and the amount would be so great as to compel us to rationalize our expenses, limit our expectations, and even deny legitimate
The Budget-Mr. Fraser
demands, while trying to set up a new economic order for and by all Canadians.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to participate in the debate on the budget. As the labour critic of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, I wish to address my attention primarily at the beginning to the remarks the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) made a few days ago in this debate. I refer especially to the following part of his speech as reported at page 4799 of Hansard:
I would like to come now to a point which is particularly important to me, that is, the co-operation among the major interest groups in the economy, those of the labour movement, business and industry, and consumer groups. We have to work out, on a voluntary basis, a process for consultation which will allow us to make the necessary adjustments to our current economic predicament and to prevent disastrous schisms between various elements of society.
My 14-point program on labour affairs is intended precisely to create a consultative council or forum which would provide facilities for bringing together representatives of the various sectors working together to diminish social conflict. The establishment of such a commission would be particularly useful in the difficult period through which we are now passing.
I suggest it is difficult for any hon. member to quarrel with the minister's objective. But I remind hon. members that the minister spoke this way some years ago. Largely as a result of his initiative, the Canada Labour Relations Council was established. The objectives of which the minister spoke were to be realized through the work of the council. But the Canadian Labour Relations Council became a defunct organization as soon as the government broke its commitment to labour that there would be no controls. It broke its commitments when it imposed controls some 18 months ago, after saying there would not be controls. Our labour people withdrew their participation in the Canada Labour Relations Council and also left the Economic Council of Canada.
What has been the result of all this? Attempts to bring various sectors of the economy together in some kind of consultative forum have been futile. Any such attempts made in the past months have failed, because of the policies espoused not just by the Minister of Labour but by the government generally. I say this advisedly and anyone examining recent history must concede that what I say is correct. We are living a year of change, something which is well recognized by that well known writer on labour matters, Ed Finn. In a column which appeared in the Toronto Star of January 3, 1977, Mr. Finn, who researches his subjects well, wrote in part:
The safest prediction is that 1977 will be a hectic bargaining year. No fewer than 630 major collective agreements-229 of them in the construction industry-will be expiring before year's end, covering more than one million workers.
In addition, about 250 sets of negotiations involving another half million employees have been carried over from 1976, and remain to be settled. So it shapes up as one of the busiest bargaining years on record.
Clearly, we have a difficult year before us. Although the government is to lift controls, it has established no mechanism for creating a climate in which we can disengage ourselves from controls without chaos. The reason for this situation is partly that the government flip-flopped on its position with regard to controls. Labour has no confidence in the government, but it must be confident that its views on the establish-
April 21, 1977

The Budget-Mr. Fraser
ment of a tripartite consultative arrangement will be accepted. Labour feels that some kind of consultative tripartite arrangement is essential if labour, government and industry are to know in which direction the economy is moving, how the economy is to be planned and how large a share of the economic pie will be available to the various sectors of our economic community. Mr. Finn went on to say in the article from which I quoted:
The CLC's proposal for a tripartite economic planning system is barely alive after a cold reception by business and government, and some back-peddling by union leaders themselves. If it is to have any hope of being considered seriously, it could only be in a climate of relative industrial peace.
It is important for members of the House, the business community and the labour community to know generally and understand well the aims of the CLC. Mr. Speaker, I ask hon. members to cast their minds back to May of last year, to the time of the CLC manifesto. There was considerable legitimate concern in this country that proposals in the manifesto for a tripartite council which would report to government and have extensive decision-making powers were unacceptable in that they went beyond the scope of the parliamentary system.
My party's position on this was made very clear at the time. The position of other parties was also made clear by their spokesmen. That position as it was originally put forward was expressed clearly in a speech by Mr. Morris of the Canadian Labour Congress. Speaking to the Trade Union Congress in Great Britain on September 9 of last year he said this:
We also adopted a policy statement, called Labour's Manifesto for Canada, which determines the general orientation of our movement and calls for the creation of a tripartite decision-making body which would have powers to plan social and economic policy, control private and public investment and supervise national income redistribution.
If we are to understand labour's point of view, it is very important to recognize that for whatever the reasons the position taken originally in May of last year and on subsequent occasions has been very considerably modified by the Canadian Labour Congress. It is important to remember this because the concept of tripartism on a consultative basis is not nearly the ogre it has been painted by some people who may have looked at the Canadian Labour Congress manifesto but clearly have not been talking to people in the labour movement in the ensuing months.
It is appropriate to point out that Mr. Morris, President of the Canadian Labour Congress, in a speech to the Canadian Club on February 21, 1977, stated very clearly the present position of the CLC on tripartism. His words ought to be recorded in Hansard and considered by all hon. members. This is the position of the Canadian Labour Congress. I quote from page 4 of Mr. Morris' speech:
What the congress has proposed to the government and to Canada is a national council for social and economic planning in which the two partners in industry-labour and management-can meet to discuss and debate the major issues which confront them. The government would be invited to sit in, either in an observer capacity or to chair the meetings. The council would be mainly advisory and consultative in nature with an independent research group attached to it and under its direction. This would guarantee that the council would have a

life of its own and would not be captive to the massive flow of government statistics and information only.
The reason it is important to recognize the position of labour is that despite difficulties with the government, labour has been moving along with representatives of the business community to reach exactly what Mr. Morris was talking about in his speech.
It is of considerable interest to all hon. members, especially those on the government side, to recognize that on October 28, 1976, the Minister of Labour made a speech to the International Federation of Chemical and General Workers' Union in which he set out his own proposal for consultation. That proposal calls for a multipartite national forum which would bring together representatives of government, labour, business,the farm community and possibly others. This multipartite body would provide decision-makers in the industrial relations field with the documents, information and recommendations they need for making decisions that are in their own interest and in the public interest.
That national forum which the Minister of Labour has been putting forward as the first plank in his 14-point program has just not come about. One can ask why it has not come about, even though the minister keeps saying it is government policy. Part of the reason is that labour has said quite clearly to the government that it does not want to meet, at least in the initial stages, in a situation where it will be outnumbered, where labour will just be another voice in a multipartite meeting with representatives from all sorts of different interests within the Canadian community. Labour wants to get at the fundamentals that have to be faced by business, labour and government, not just with respect to the state of industrial relations but with respect to what is a fair and equitable approach to the economy of this country.
Questions have been asked in this House by myself and others for a number of weeks and months in an attempt to find out whether what the minister proposed as his national forum in October is still government policy. In answer to questions which I directed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) he said what really amounts to this, "It is too early to talk about multipartite arrangements".
In an effort to try to find out whether the Minister of Labour is actually putting together any multipartite forum it is interesting to look at the chronology of events. On November 27 last I asked the minister who would compose this national forum. I asked if the minister could say whether the Canadian Labour Congress accepted the format on the national forum as he had set it out. The minister replied as follows:
We are not sure at this stage whether the type of forum we are suggesting-an alliance of various interests on an equal footing to discuss national problems- would be suitable to the business community or to labour.
That was on November 27, a full month after the minister had announced that his policy was to establish this national forum. He admitted that at that stage he did not have the agreement of labour. It is impossible to put anything together on a voluntary basis with labour unless there is acceptance of the format in which labour is to be asked to function. The
April 21, 1977

minister insists upon going on with this concept of a national forum although it is apparent that he cannot put it together.
On November 29 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) was asked about this. He said at a meeting with representatives of the business community:
-but they were positive about participation in a multipartite group which would make it possible to have discussions and perhaps agreement on some of the major economic questions-
Of course, I was not at the meeting to which the minister referred, nor did I have any chance to be privy to the proceedings. However, if you talk to business leaders and businessmen it is quite clear there is no unanimity at the moment by the business community that at this stage, at least, they want to get involved in a national forum such as the minister has described. On December 3 another question was put to the Minister of Labour by myself. I asked:
-will the minister now please tell the House what other parties the government will be talking to, to whom he referred in his answers a few days ago and whether he has told labour what other parties he has in mind?
He was unable to set out what other parties he was referring to, he said:
We do not know whether there is going to be some real participation by, for instance, labour.
It is rather incredible that on October 28 government policy was set out by the minister calling for this national forum, and two months later he admitted he did not know whether labour would take advantage of it. I repeat, the minister will not be able to put together the national forum he talks about, which is the first plank in his 14-points program, unless he has the agreement and consent of labour. As I said before, from what I can learn from discussions with business leaders there is no way labour is going to sit down at a multipartite arrangement in which they do not have a significant role to play and are on some kind of equal basis with the other two partners with whom they are prepared to discuss the matter, that is, industry and government.
The minister made matters no better by his inept attack on the relationship between the Canadian Labour Congress and the New Democratic Party. It is no secret to anybody who has studied labour history that such a relationship exists. It is a special relationship. It has to be respected and, above all, it is not one which a minister of labour trying to seek the co-operation of labour ought to be attacking, ridiculing or using in any way to embarrass the very people with whom he must deal.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I notice that some members to my left support what I have said. Mr. Speaker, this relationship between the CLC and the NDP is one of the realities of life, and it amazes me that the Minister of Labour could be so insensitive, particularly at a time when it is necessary to arrange for accommodation and discussion, and that an attack on such partnership should be put into the mix.
The Budget-Mr. A. Lambert
I should like, now, to refer to another incident of the same kind. Following a meeting between labour, business representatives and the government a few weeks ago, some altogether unnecessary and unwise statements were made, primarily by the Minister of Finance. I have to be frank here and point out that the Minister of Labour was incorrectly quoted at the time. But the Minister of Finance said at the time that commitments had been received from labour leaders to speak out on the need for restraint. That was foolish, because such commitments had not been made and, of course, labour leaders immediately had to deny making statements of that kind.
It is easy to ask why no commitment had been made by labour leaders along these lines, but it will harm none of us to understand why there could not be any such commitment at that point. These men are executive officers of the CLC and they cannot walk out of a secret meeting and start to announce policy or concessions in advance of consultations with their unions. If a Minister of the Crown does not understand this, it is no wonder the government has difficulty in establishing rapport with labour representatives.
This is just one more incident in a series of inept actions over the last several years which have made it difficult to put together the results the minister says he wants to achieve. Whatever may be the result of this debate, it is necessary for government members to be much more careful and understand the situation better that they seem to. They must show themselves more sensitive toward politics in the labour family. They must understand that labour in Canada no longer wants to be brought to the railway committee room once a year to present a brief to the Prime Minister, be photographed with members of the cabinet and then told to go away for another 12 months. Nor, for that matter, do they want to carry on as they have in the past several years, speaking to the business sector through press releases and columns in the newspapers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. The time allotted to the hon. member has expired.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I wonder if I might continue for a few moments, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There was an order of the House yesterday that speeches would be limited to 20 minutes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in the budget debate, I would like to express my views as briefly and objectively but also as frankly as possible. Obviously, I have criticisms to make but also suggestions to present, which I consider as valid and which may help check this terrifying unemployment crisis which affects young workers particularly. I know that many industrialized countries are presently experiencing a very high rate of unemployment but merely stating that the economic situation is not better elsewhere will not solve our problems. We are living in Canada, it is our country which is in trouble. We must take up the challenge right here so that our vast and resourceful country
4870

April 21, 1977
The Budget-Mr. A. Lambert
can provide each Canadian with the opportunity to make an honest living.
Mr. Speaker, it is impossible to discuss the present budget without reference to money. Indeed, this year's budget, as the previous ones, is merely an alignment of figures representing dollars under two distinct headings, incoming and outgoing. I heard a backbencher on the government side a moment ago say that we keep repeating the same hackneyed phrases. If he thinks that his argument will change our approach when dealing with the shortcomings and flaws of our financial system, he is wrong. We take the same stand, because the government keeps making the same mistakes over and over again. To convince ourselves of this, all we have to do is read over the speeches of various ministers of finances, Messrs. Benson, Turner or Macdonald.
I remember among other things, Mr. Speaker, that one year Mr. Turner introduced an anti-inflation budget, at the risk, as he said, of increasing the unemployment rate, and, the following year, he presented a new budget which was supposed to fight unemployment, at the risk of fanning inflation. You need only read over his speeches to see that I am saying the truth.
As a result, Mr. Speaker, inflation kept increasing and so did unemployment, which proves the inefficiency of both systems. That is why I am saying there is no risk in trying the solutions proposed by the Social Credit of Canada, which consist, among other things, in financing the public sector through the Bank of Canada, granting a discount on Canadian products and a national dividend to every Canadian, in order to increase the family income, without having to increase retail prices to the consumer.
In refusing to tackle the situation, the government had to make compromises on both sides, on the right as well as on the left, and it does not seem to realize that a country cannot prosper, if there is not enough work for its industry and labour force, and if the national debt is constantly increasing to the benefit of finance companies, instead of using the national bank, which is in fact the people's bank, to meet its financial needs. I know that at times ministers chide members on this side of the House for accusing the government of spending too much and, in the same breath, for requesting increased funds for old age security, rebates on milk products and Canadian products, national dividends and pensions at 60 years of age.
As far as I am concerned, I blame the government for indebting the country for things we could now do without so as to have more money for more important sectors. I will give an example of that-the national debt service for which we will pay $700 million more this year. For the financial year 1976-77, we paid $4.65 billion in interest while this year we will be required to pay $5.35 billion.
I suggest that if the government were to regain control over credit money within the nation to finance the public sector, it would thus save a lot of money in interest which could be used for public works, for repairing and building wharves, for

improving municipal airports and for many other public facilities.
The Department of National Defence got an increase of $414 million; yet, we are not at war. To my mind, we would be well advised to take part of that amount to help finance the housing program which would create jobs while giving Canadians additional housing. The other part could be assigned to the Canada Works Program: many sponsors have been disappointed to see well-prepared and serious projects denied.
We must recognize the fact that mechanization and automation replace man. That has been proved. A few years ago, it was claimed that it had yet to be proved that the machine was replacing man. Learned economists told us that for a given production, a number equal to that of the men who lost their jobs to machines were being employed in manufacturing those machines. In other words, they claimed that the machine does not replace man but displace him only. With passing years, the capacity for material production increases. And in the meantime, fewer man-hours go into every unit of production, or expressed otherwise, there is more production to buy and lower total salaries to buy. That is one of the causes of unemployment.
The total salary can no longer buy the total production. Between the two, there is a difference which must be compensated. Various means are available to us to achieve this. First, an extensive program of public works aimed at providing jobs, therefore incomes, without necessarily producing consumer goods. Second, providing dividends to each and every Canadian would increase his purchasing power without raising prices and allow him to benefit from surpluses; and through a discount on all Canadian goods.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that we should finance consumption if we want our economic life to resume its normal course, and the domestic market is still the most stable one. As I was saying, there must be another income in addition to salary. Though labour unions may do their utmost to increase wages, they will never fill the void between the income earned and the total cost of production. Therefore, another solution must be found. Mankind has set up an incredible production system but it has yet to devise a fair distribution system. We must develop a new economic system to get our country out of the rut, and that is what I think the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Tessier) said earlier in his speech.
As regards private assets, we should invent another revenue for each Canadian by distributing new money based on the missing equivalent between the total value of products and the total value of wages. Major Douglas proposes as a solution the national dividend and the discount.
As regards public assets, we will have to answer yes to the four following questions: Are those works necessary? Do we have the material to execute them? Do we have the required labour? Do we have the equipment to help the workers in their job? If we can give an affirmative answer to those questions, we will have to execute the work without asking ourselves whether we have the money. Money should be immediately available through new votes, not borrowed from the private

sector. I suggest that Canada should have its own merchant marine. That is another honest suggestion I am making to the government. We already have shipyards, as well as workers capable of building very good ships. We could therefore orient ourselves gradually in that direction. At the present time, our country pays subsidies to our shipyards which build ships for foreign countries, and that, in order to give work to our people. Why not use that money to build ourselves a good merchant marine?
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to share another idea with the government; it seems quite feasible to me and would improve things in several regards. I know there are people who will be startled when they read this, but I could not care less because even Pasteur, when he gave mankind his formula for pasteurization, was scoffed at; yet, today, everyone uses it.
Mr. Speaker, bearing in mind that we have fairly severe winters and that the snow is usually quite abundant, especially in eastern Quebec, consequently road maintenance is very costly since snow must be removed to facilitate the use of motor vehicles. Because of our climate, the cost of road construction is very high and every possible means should be taken to ensure that roads are properly built in order to lower maintenance costs. Mr. Speaker, I have noticed while driving on the highway in winter that trees along the road make for much less drifting, less snow on the pavement and much safer driving.
Since highways come under provincial jurisdiction, I suggest that the federal government submit to the provinces a joint plan to plant trees along completed highways like the trans-Canada highway. When those trees have reached a certain height, not only will they be a pleasing sight, but hopefully they will help, first, to reduce maintenance costs. Second, with less snow on the roadway, visibility will be improved since the trees will reduce drifting, and there is every reason to believe that there would be fewer accidents, and then insurance rates could go down. Fewer accidents causing costly material damages would obviously result in lower transportation costs which would help small and medium-sized business in outlying areas to compete with businesses in large centres.
1 am thinking, Mr. Speaker, especially of the south shore and the far eastern part of Quebec, as well as of the Mari-times. God knows that we have trouble setting up and maintaining industries to provide employment in these areas of high unemployment. Third, this tree planting program along highways would help create summer jobs for students and for a number of other workers who have trouble finding jobs. It would also be a worthwhile project from which the people would benefit eventually. Fourth, since trees serve two other major purposes in nature, it is advisable, in my opinion, that young people be aware of this so that they may contribute to their protection and ensure their development.
It is a known fact that tree roots make some kind of natural filter and improve the quality of water. Woods and trees also help to maintain the underground water at a higher level.
The Budget-Mr. A. Lambert
Many communities are now faced with a shortage of drinking water and that it costs millions of dollars to lay down water-pipes often over very long distances. Tree-cutting and drainage lower the water level.
Fifth, since we use pollutants for road maintenance in winter, tree planting along the roads would also fight the pollution caused by such chemicals. Mr. Speaker, I feel that for all these reasons, the government should seriously consider this suggestion and try to implement it starting with the areas most affected by severe winter weather conditions.
Since private enterprise is unable to take care of all the labour available and it is very bad for a developing country like Canada to have one million unemployed, it is therefore the government's duty to step in and carry out worthwhile public works. Let us keep in mind the proverb: Idleness is the root of all evil. Now, evil can only be rooted out through the wise use of human resources, and the oldest formula known to date is work. I feel that when the entire population will be put to work, we shall need fewer jails. And it would be a saving as it costs $15,000 a year for each inmate. There would also be fewer nervous breakdowns caused to many people by a lack of revenue to meet their needs. It would also help reduce hospitalization costs as it is generally recognized that work is a good health factor. Hon. members who are working very hard are in good health.
It is also through work that we can boost our gross national product on which our monetary system is based, for it rather than gold determines the real value of our currency. The government should not increase only the gross national debt. It should also expand the gross national production and raise the revenues of the working class. Low income earners are the main victims of inflation and unemployment.
To come back to our gross national debt, it climbs discouragingly but nobody seems overly concerned. According to an official document tabled in the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, we can see that this debt on March 31, 1968 was $42 billion, $78 billion in 1975, close to $89 billion in 1976-almost $4,000 per capita. Think about it, a jump of $46 billion over an eight year period. No wonder the 1977-78 budget sets aside over $5 billion for interests, more than $16 million a day.
Mr. Speaker, such is the result of a broken down and obsolete financial system. Canada has an urgent need for leaders able to fight the financial dictatorship. This dictatorship is the main cause of all our national economic difficulties. This government should officially answer the following question before Parliament: Who creates our Canadian money supply, the government of private banks? If the government makes all our monetary stock as many people believe, why does it borrow from private sources billion of dollars on which it pays interest?
In a speech before the Union commerciale mauricienne in November 1959, former minister of finance Donald Fleming said this: I want to emphasize that the Canadian government has absolutely no control over our money supply. It can neither increase nor reduce it. That, Mr. Speaker, is a very clear
80012-30'/2

April 21, 1977
The Budget-Mr. A. Lambert
recognition by the government that it has surrendered that important responsibility to financial institutions. I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are preparing to inform me that my time has expired, but if you will allow me to continue, I have very interesting things to say to the House which, I think, will not waste its time. So, I was saying that as early as 1931-
