subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I still want things to be in order. Yesterday an agreement was reached under which it was not clearly established whether the hon. member would have 20, 22 or 30 minutes. I am therefore willing to ignore the clock for a minute or two, hoping that he will stay within 20 or 30 minutes, which will be agreeable to all other members who also want to speak before 9.45 p.m.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank the Chair and all my colleagues. I once said that we could speak more rapidly and I want to repeat that it is possible. But since the standing orders did allow more time, I acted accordingly and this is why I would like to finish very briefly.
I said a while ago that as early as 1931-quite before our time-Pope Pius XI had denounced the financial dictatorship in the following terms: Those who control credit somewhat control the economic blood of the nation so that without their permission it is impossible to breathe. This is still true today. When we advocate a monetary and financial reform, financiers say that it is quite a complicated field, that it has never been done elsewhere. Mr. Speaker, I feel that it is not worthy of a Canadian to show suh an inferiority complex. We must have the courage to innovate in that field. After all, we are not monkeys, as the late Real Caouette used to say. He was brave enough to be true to himself without aping others. If he were here today, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that he would openly advocate the same reforms with the same courage.
Last December I pledged in the House to remain faithful to the principles of Social Credit and to the memory of Real Caouette and till someone comes up with a better formula ensuring a more equitable distribution, I shall fight for the ideals for which that great Canadian, Real Caouette, fought all his life. There was no atomic bomb at the outset of the war in 1939, yet atoms exist since the beginning of time. They tackled the problem and after six years, finally produced the first A bomb. They decided to do it, yet it was harder to bring about than the monetary reform we are advocating.
Armstrong was the first man on the moon, yet it presented more problems than the reform of our monetary and financial systems so that they serve the people and not the other way around. Armstrong did not say: Nobody went there before, so neither will I. He accepted the challenge and went.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I deplore the fact that the 1977-78 budget does not provide an income tax cut for small wage earners while this category is hardest hit by inflation. We must keep in mind that inflation is the rightful heir to the current financial system before which the government bows down low, while Canadians bear its consequences.
In conclusion, once more I urge all those listening tonight and those who will read these words to assume their respon-

sibilities, some of which are considerable, and fill the mission for which they were elected, that is to exercise the right to govern for the common good of all by acting as impartial referees to protect the meek. It is the only way, Mr. Speaker, to save our democracy. Let us act while there is still time. That is the watchword I wanted to give my colleagues so that together we examine closely the question of financing the public sector and if we resolve to propose solutions, the government and all hon. members will certainly rejoice along with the entire population because, by so doing, we will check inflation and enable all Canadians who have enough guts to want to work, to find a job and be productive.
That is what the people of our country expect from members of parliament, and I hope that in the following days we shall set to work seriously and get something done to stand up against those financial institutions whose only goal is to make profits, instead of serving the public seriously.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. C. Abbott (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a day of such profound and positive political excitement I know a speech on the budget will probably lack the kind of attraction for public notice that would ordinarily be the case, judging from some of the speeches we heard this afternoon.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tell us what you really think of the budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think it will not have escaped your notice, Mr. Speaker, that several objectives of the government's economic policy as enunciated by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), in his address and supported by specific budgetary measures, are also related to proposed changes to competition policy in Bill C-42.
The minister pointed out that the recent decline in the value of the Canadian dollar, partly reflecting lower interest rates in Canada, can be of benefit to Canadian firms by helping them to offset high costs. The change in the exchange rate will provide them with new opportunities to compete with now higher-priced imports at home and high prices in markets abroad. The Minister of Finance noted that these benefits are ours to seize, but only if we keep our domestic costs and prices firmly in check. This is where an important contribution can be made by the proposed amendments to the law on competition which I introduced in the House a month ago.
There are too many industries in Canada which have been able to pursue, as a traditional pricing strategy, the adoption of the U.S. price, plus the tariff, plus transportation costs in establishing the going price in Canada. If such industries now do not strongly resist cost increases, they will quickly dissipate the advantage which the decline in the value of the dollar has provided. It is my belief that industries in which competition is not very vigorous are less likely to resist cost increases because they can anticipate the passing on of such increases to buyers without too much trouble. The strengthened Competition Act
April 21, 1977

will encourage more effective competition, which can be expected to make the passing on of cost increases more difficult.
Bill C-42 takes account of the need to improve the competitive position of Canadian industry at home and abroad in specific ways. Under the provisions of the bill, mergers which are seriously anti-competitive will be blocked, but mergers which are likely to bring about substantial gains in efficiency will not be prohibited by the competition board where any anti-competitive effects fall short of virtual monopoly.
Even where a virtual monopoly is likely to result, the board may still permit the merger to proceed, to take advantage of the efficiency gains, provided suitable safeguards can be prescribed. In addition, specialization agreements may be permitted, either absolutely or conditionally, where otherwise unobtainable substantial gains in efficiency are likely. Similarly, the broadening and clarification of the export exemption should remove the fears of businessmen about entering into export agreements, to our benefit as a trading nation. Thus, the investment incentives offered business by this budget, along with the opportunities for both increased exportation and import substitution afforded by the decline in the value of the Canadian dollar, are reinforced by direct government encouragement of, and support for, enhanced efficiency.
Of course, opportunities for exports and access to needed imports can be frustrated by international cartels or allocation of world markets between affiliates of multinational enterprises. No budget measure can easily deal with these restraints. Competition policy can, however, proscribe such practices and Bill C-42 contains several provisions of this kind. Canadian firms participating directly in international conspiracies, if they account for half or more of domestic production or supply of the product involved, are to be subject to criminal prosecution.
In the case of agreements or communications between a Canadian firm and a foreign affiliate to restrict imports into, or exports from, Canada for the purpose of protecting price levels here or abroad, the competition board may prohibit the agreement or the implementation of the communication whenever the Canadian firm accounts for 25 per cent or more of domestic production or supply of the product involved.
These and other measures are designed to protect Canadian production and employment from artificial restraints on exports and Canadian consumers from exploitation by artificial restraints on imports. They are a Canadian contribution to the international effort directed against private restrictions on world trade, and thus to the goal of a freer world trading environment cited by the Minister of Finance.
Another feature of the budget is to make changes affecting the financing of small business. Certainly, tax policies affect their efficiency and ability to compete, and I welcome the changes introduced by my colleague. Also affecting competitive relationships in the market, the amendments to the combines act are of paramount importance. The strengthening of the conspiracy provisions dealing with price fixing and market sharing as a result of the stage one revisions of the combines
The Budget-Mr. Abbott
act will provide the small businessman with more assurance than he had previously of being able to buy in competitive markets.
Likewise, the strengthening of the provision on price maintenance means that the small businessman will be protected from any attempt by suppliers to assert control over his pricing policy. Under the "refusal to deal" provisions of state one the small businessman has some recourse when he is refused supply of a commodity or service because of the non-competitive or monopolistic character of the supplying industry.
The further strengthening of the competition law proposed in the stage two legislation -will play an important role in protecting small and medium-sized businesses in Canada from anti-competitive practices of larger firms which possess market power. The stage two proposals should improve significantly the business environment in which small and medium-sized businesses operate. They will do this by removing or reducing artificial barriers which block or inhibit small firms from either expanding in the market or entering new businesses as effective competitors.
The purpose of the legislation is to encourage a flexible and dynamic economy in which the decisions about whether businesses will succeed are made to the greatest extent possible by the market and not by firms or groups of firms seeking to protect the status quo as expressed in their market shares. Any firm, whether small or large, that has a better product or a better way of doing business should not fail because artificial barriers to competition have inhibited its ability to offer its products for sale in the Canadian marketplace. There are many Canadian industries in which a small number of large firms account for a very high proportion of the total output and sales of the industry, and this makes the stage two proposals of particular importance for small and medium-sized firms.
My colleague also noted that control of government spending is an integral part of our anti-inflation policies, providing room for the growth of business investment and job creation. The measures in Bill C-42 which I have already mentioned also stimulate job creation by promoting efficiency in private industry, thus increasing employment through improved competitiveness. Another feature of the bill also makes a contribution to our anti-inflation efforts-the provisions concerning regulated conduct.
Just as we seek to control government spending, we seek here to limit the scope of regulation to what is necessary and to promote as far as possible the principles of allocative efficiency and competition in areas under federal regulation. The criteria proposed in the bill for conferring an exemption from the combines act on persons subject to regulation all serve to impose public accountability on public monopolies. Moreover, the requirement that federal regulatory agencies exercise their powers, when alternatives exist, in the manner least restrictive of competition will respond to the criticism that government

April 21, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Abbott
regulation has suppressed market processes and has sometimes been a significant cause of inflation.
[ Translation]
It is no coincidence if the budget proposals and the provisions of the competition bill complete and strengthen one another. This is the result, not only of the policy, but of the economic strategy the government is putting forward. In an editorial, Claude Ryan referred to Bill C-42 in Le Devoir of 17 March as " ... one with the most far-reaching consequences, and one that most clearly reflects the government's plans for the economy".
Complete freedom of action without rules is the fastest way for the powerful to swallow the weak. Such spiralling concentration is soon detrimental to the public interest. On the other hand, because of our small Canadian markets, we must allow for concentration of economic power for the purpose of achieving economies of scale and offering more goods of higher quality. This also allows Canadian companies to be more competitive on world markets and therefore to employ more people and produce more goods.
These two aspects of our economic life can be controlled by a set of government measures. Both the competition policy and the fiscal and monetary policy fit into that framework. Here is how Mr. Ryan describes the situation: "There is quite a number of tools available to governments to meet the problem. From income tax through the various specialized regulating bodies to the increasing forms of government involvement as an entrepreneur, there is quite a number of initiatives governments use to limit the excessive lust for economic power felt by many groups, and foster a more equitable distribution of wealth than the market forces alone would permit. In this gamut, there is a special place for measures to harness more directly the economic power such as in our current Combines Investigation Act."

Mr. Speaker, on previous occasions I have spoken of my department's overriding concern with the effectiveness of the market and its capacity to meet the needs and aspirations of producers and consumers alike. From this vantage point I am extremely sensitive to the personal hardship and the very serious long-term damage that can be wrought by uncontrolled inflationary pressures. The budgetary address by my colleague indicates a clear awareness of these dangers and a recognition of the vital importance of prudent economic management. Canadian consumers will certainly share in the benefits that accrue from this policy approach. They will benefit, as well, from the tariff adjustments announced in the budget which support this government's over-all pursuit of a more liberal trading environment.
In considering the budget measures we should take account of the fact that they are only one facet of government economic policy, a vitally important one, to be sure, but requiring help from and co-ordination with numerous other aspects. I am pleased to speak in support of them today, and I am equally pleased to be able to reinforce them with strong legislation
[Mr. Abbott.)
standing in my name. I commend them to the House for its consideration.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will address myself to what in my view is the maladministration of the revenue side of the government. My colleagues have dealt with the budget generally, pitiful document that it is, and how it fails to fulfil the needs of Canadians. I have just 20 minutes, Mr. Speaker. I was not here yesterday, and if I had been I would not have given unanimous consent to restricting speeches to 20 minutes. It is an outrage that when you are absent from this place-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member does not have the right to criticize decisions of the House of which he is a member. All hon. members are supposed to be in the House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I may not have the right to criticize actions of the House, but surely I can express my opinion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member cannot express his opinions on a decision that has been made by the House. He will find that out quickly if he reads the rules.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then I will express it outside the chamber, Mr. Speaker. In any event, I only have 20 minutes to speak and not 45 as I had anticipated.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Thank God.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is supposed to be a document of the government of the just society, and I want to examine one area of that government's administration to see how just it is to society. There are 8,930,000 taxpayers in Canada, people who paid personal income tax in 1974. In my view, this government has failed to collect income tax fairly, efficiently and with impartiality as the facts that I will recite will show. In 1976, at the end of March, the government collected in excess of $17 billion in income tax from individuals from across Canada; eight million people paid income tax.
I have here a document put out by the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin), entitled "Inside Taxation". This document is well put together and reads well. I should like to read from page 34 where it is stated that in the year ended March 31, 1976, the department issued close to 11.5 million notices of assessment. In the same period, approximately 13,500 notices of objection were received with about 93 per cent of them being settled without litigation. The Department of Justice, tax litigation section, is responsible for providing all legal services and advice required by the appeals branch in disposing of notices of objection, in appeals to the tax review board, the Federal Court of Canada and the Supreme Court of Canada.
April 21, 1977

What I am going to say relates to the Department of Justice and the Department of National Revenue. On page 28 we are informed that forceful procedures are available to taxation collectors to use against those taxpayers who do not pay voluntarily, and that taxes are collected by means of wage garnishments from other income or bank deposits or through the seizure and sale of assets, or both. That is the principle that this document gives. It goes on to say that during appeal periods the amount assessed must be paid, whether or not there is an objection or appeal outstanding. Whether or not you appeal, whether you object or not, you have to pay your taxes and the interest.
In certain circumstances the department may accept collateral security for the amount of a debt until the issue is resolved. In my experience, the collateral security is a bond from a bonding company fully covering the amount that the department claims is owing in interest and penalties. That is what the ordinary taxpayer has to observe-that is what the people whom I have come across in my practice as a lawyer, have to observe. Why is one particular taxpayer in Canada allowed to get away without observing these rules? That is what I am going to deal with today.
On March 31, 1977, Mr. Speaker, there were nine appeals before the Supreme Court of Canada dealing with the Income Tax Act waiting for a hearing, and one appeal waiting for a judgment. So there were ten appeals from taxpayers before the Supreme Court of Canada. There were 77 appeals before the Federal Court of Appeal; 66 waiting for hearings, two waiting for judgments, and in nine the judgments were given but they were waiting for the appeal time limit to expire. There were 77 cases before the Federal Court of Appeal, 671 cases before the Federal Court of Canada, and ten cases before the Supreme Court of Canada, for a total of 758 cases.
One of the appeals before the Supreme Court of Canada has been there since October, 1970, without anything being done about it. It want to know why seven years should be allowed to go after a notice of appeal was given in the Supreme Court of Canada by John Christopher Doyle and yet the Crown has not proceeded or forced him to proceed, or asked the court to dismiss the appeal. I want to know why some $4.5 million should be owing to the government in income tax, penalties and interest, and still be unpaid. These appeals deal with the taxation years 1950 and 1954-27 and 23 years ago.
This matter went before the Income Tax Appeal Board in 1967. The taxpayer lost his appeal. He then took it to the Exchequer Court of Canada in 1970 when Mr. Justice Gibson brought down judgment in two appeals which are on the public record-Doyle v. M.N.R. (1970) Dominion Tax Cases, page 6251, which relates to the income tax year 1950 and held that $200,000 had to be added to his income for that year. Mr. Justice Gibson of the Exchequer Court dismissed the appeal. In 1970 Dominion Tax Cases, page 6262, Doyle vs M.N.R. relating to 1954 income, Mr. Justice Gibson held that $2,080,000 had to be added to the taxpayer's income for that year and tax had to be paid on that amount. His income had previously
The Budget-Mr. Crosbie
been seen to be $198,173. The reassessed tax was $1,859,000. Sixteen years after 1954, judgment was delivered, on June 29, 1970.
That was bad enough, Mr. Speaker, but the next thing that happened was that leave to appeal was applied for and granted in October, 1970 six years and eight months ago. The relevant file is Supreme Court No. 12028/9. Every year since-and certainly this happened last year-the taxpayer has applied to the Supreme Court for his case to be taken off the list, and representatives of the Department of National Revenue have concurred. What is going on, Mr. Speaker? This would not happen for you or me, so what are the exceptional circumstances here?
John Christopher Doyle is a fugitive from justice in Canada and in the United States. He has control of a Canadian company incorporated under the Federal Corporation Tax Act known as Canadian Javelin Limited. He owns 18.2 per cent of the shares of that company, which gives him control because the other shares are widely distributed. For 25 years he has despoiled that company despite the best efforts of the Securities Exchange Commission and others to stop him. The company has been raped repeatedly. The Canadian authorities have failed to act to protect the shareholders. There are some
30.000	shareholders altogether, some 65 per cent of them being American. Mr. Doyle has 1,319,000 shares of Canadian Javelin Limited, and the public record shows that the government holds 125,000 of those shares for the income tax owed to the government. As far as I know, Mr. Doyle has been allowed to vote those shares down through the years to help him keep control of the company he is despoiling.
In 1965 the government issued a writ of extent against Canadian Javelin Limited presumably for the moneys it owed to Mr. Doyle, or to inform the company that they should not pay such moneys to him but should pay them to the Crown, against this judgment. Canadian Javelin Limited ignored these attachments. The company's records show that it is contingently liable for $525,055 which it paid to Mr. Doyle despite the writ of extent.
What else happened in connection with this feeble attempt by the Government of Canada to collect the moneys owing to it and get some security? Apparently they did not get the other
1.319.000	shares that Mr. Doyle owned, although he was in Canada all during that period. He is not here now but is a fugitive from justice. To get around the injunction that Canadian Javelin Limited should not pay him any moneys, he set up a company in the Bahamas called Javelin Export Limited. This company performed so-called consultant services for Canadian Javelin Limited. The sequence is that Canadian Javelin Limited pays Javelin Export Limited for these services, and in turn it pays Mr. Doyle. But Mr. Doyle is not paying a cent in Canadian taxes today, and has not paid for years. Using that simple device, he is receiving income from a Canadian company which receives most of its income from the Wabysh Mine Iron Ore Company's property in Labrador.
The government is standing by, is sitting by, is slinking by, and has slunk by for the last 14 years, allowing this to go on.

April 21, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Crosbie
This calls for an explanation, Mr. Speaker, and we have not received one. I put a question on the order paper on February 8; I put a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) early in February; I wrote to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) on March 23, 1977, informing them of this situation, but I have not had an answer from anyone. I am not going to let this drop, Mr. Speaker; I do not see why I should. Why should one taxpayer, and he a fugitive from justice, be allowed this 16-year leeway by the Liberal government? There is misfeasance, malfeasance, or some kind of feasance involved here, Mr. Speaker.
I am only getting warmed up, Mr. Speaker, but I see time is passing and there is a lot more information to come yet.
On February 8 this year I put a question on the order paper. On February 10 Mr. Doyle's appeal was again removed from the Supreme Court registry at the request of his solicitor, and neither the Department of National Revenue nor the Department of Justice did anything about that. What is going on here, Mr. Speaker? Why should the taxpayers of Canada pay up and have their arms twisted, and perhaps have the bailiff sent into their homes and their assets seized, yet one man is allowed to get away with this?
I have not got time to go into the machinations of Canadian Javelin Limited, Mr. Speaker, but they would shock the House. Its shares were once worth $18 each, but they have been delisted from stock exchanges. Trading in them has been suspended, and according to last trading reports those shares were worth $1.55 each, in Canada. That has happened because of the despoliation of the company by Mr. Doyle and his group. Therefore the 125,000 shares the government holds as security have declined in value from $18 each to $1.55. Does this not show negligence? Does this not demand an explanation?
In 1974 Mr. Doyle was paid $118,750 by Javelin Export Limited, which got the money from Canadian Javelin Limited. In 1975 he was paid $100,600 by the Javelin Export Company, which got the money from Canadian Javelin. Mr. Speaker, all these transactions make a mockery of our laws. He was paid down in the Bahamas, where he pays no income tax. That gentleman at one time was a Canadian citizen, but I am informed that he is going to become or has become a Panamanian citizen. He has taken out those papers to have a better chance of not being extradited to Canada for the offences with which he is charged. He has not been in Canada for several years. He has paid no Canadian taxes, and either is or is about to become a citizen of Panama.
What is the answer? The two ministers to whom I wrote have not told me why the Department of Justice and the Department of National Revenue have been so dilatory in this matter. Surely the government has enough lawyers with which to pursue this matter quickly. The government employs enough lawyers to fill this House ten times. Why did the Minister of National Revenue or her representatives agree to

the postponement of the appeal? Surely if the Minister of Justice and the Minister of National Revenue were doing their job properly they would instruct their lawyers to ask the Supreme Court of Canada to tell the appellant to bring forward his factum and have his appeal heard, or have the appeal dismissed altogether. That way the process would be over.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why has the government not taken other steps to secure its investment? Why was not Mr. Doyle asked to pay income tax and the interest penalty back in 1954, 1967, 1970, 1971, 1975, or 1976?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a scandal.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This matter cries out for investigation, Mr. Speaker. Why was Mr. Doyle allowed to get away with his transparent devices? Mr. Doyle carries on, on his merry way; he does not have to obey Canadian law, criminal or civil. But he goes on taking his moneys out, not paying Canadian tax, nor even paying tax for those two particular years previously mentioned.
I do not have time to recount everything that has happened in connection with Canadian Javelin Limited. But their carryings-on would open your eyes. You would be astonished to note what has happened to the assets of that company. Most of the company's revenue has come from the iron ore deposits of Labrador. And, Mr. Speaker, there was $3,900,000 paid out for a worthless piece of paper to a company in Lichtenstein by Canadian Javelin Limited. The Lichtenstein company called, I think, Society Trans-shipping, got a letter from the then premier of Newfoundland saying they had 10,000 square miles of timber rights. In law that letter was not worth one iota, jot or tittle. The company had no right to that timber.
That letter was sold by Society Trans-shipping of Lichtenstein to Canadian Javelin Limited for more than $3,900,000. The money was taken out of the company. And we do not know who Society Trans-shipping of Lichtenstein is. Mr. Speaker, the amount paid was $3,997,500.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Bring it up with Tony Abbott.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On May 21, 1976, Mr. Doyle's lawyer in Nassau sent a letter to Canadian Javelin Limited saying that he was owed $3,278,000 by Canadian Javelin, that being income Javelin Export had promised him. That was the amount Javelin Export had promised him over the years. Apparently Canadian Javelin owed the money to Javelin Export. In any event this money, according to the lawyer, was owing to Mr. Doyle. That was another method of getting more money out of Canadian Javelin Limited, on none of which Mr. Doyle intended to pay Canadian taxes.
Despite all the money which has been pouring into the company, Canadian Javelin has not paid its shareholders a dividend for ten years. I say it is time the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) acted to protect the
April 21, 1977

shareholders of the company by appointing a receiver. The minister should have the assets of the company frozen and appoint a receiver to look after Canadian Javelin Limited to protect what is left of the company, and to protect the 30,000 odd shareholders and creditors of that company. If the minister does not have the power now to do it, this House ought to give him the power. Mr. Speaker, this is an outrageous, tragic, terrible situation and should not be allowed to go unchallenged under Canadian law. After all the company was incorporated under Canadian companies legislation. It is disgraceful that a director of that company should be able to take money out of Canada year after year without paying tax. The writ the federal government issued in 1965 is of no purpose or use whatsoever.
Apparently the hon. member has corrected a number of things on the record.

Yes, I have corrected a number of things. I am asking the government now to correct a few matters in the administration of the Department of National Revenue. Let us see that justice is done. I should like the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Justice to tell this House what they propose to do about this situation. I want the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to show us some teeth in Canadian corporate laws. The Securities and Exchange Commission of the United States is trying to remedy this situation. It has taken civil action.
What's the matter, then, with our government?

But in this country no action at all has been taken. A group of directors of Canadian Javelin Limited not under Mr. Doyle's control acquired control of the company for a six-month period last year and instituted remedial court action. They began to clean up the company. Unfortunately at a shareholders' meeting last summer where proxies were exercised, Mr. Doyle's group was voted back to power in the company. Once again Mr. Doyle appointed his puppet directors to the board of that company. Once again he controls the company, one member of the board being a member of the other place. The chairman of the board of directors is S. Fournier of the other place. As I say, that puppet board of directors once more controls Canadian Javelin.
The former board of directors instituted law suits involving millions of dollars. I do not know what has happened to those law suits. In the United States the Securities and Exchange Commission has instituted civil action. In this country we seem powerless to do anything. Why? Surely there is law covering the situation? I know there is. Mr. Speaker, I know that the powers exist under the Income Tax Act. The government's powers under the income tax legislation are savage. If the department feels you owe it any money, it can seize your assets and place attachments on your property without going through the courts. I have had some experience of this. They say that you must pay what you owe them, together with interest and penalty, before you can even proceed with your appeal.
The Budget-Mr. Crosbie
I am concerned about the protection of law abiding citizens who live and work in this country, and whose assets are here. Their families are here. Why was an international, corporate scallywag, who I do not think is a native born Canadian, allowed to fleece tens of thousands of United States and Canadian citizens? Why is he allowed to owe income tax from 1950, and from 1954? Why has this continued, despite judgments handed down by the Income Tax Appeal Board? And these judgments I might add, are slow enough in coming down.
The Income Tax Appeal Board was asked to rule 17 years after 1950 and 13 years after 1954. Three years later the Exchequer Court handed down its judgment. According to the court, the man in question owed over $3 million. Now the amount is over $4 million, if you include interest. And the government sits back and does nothing. What is wrong? I call on the Ministers of National Revenue, Justice, and Consumer and Corporate Affairs to provide the answer. Let them answer the question I have raised today. I have written about this matter to two ministers opposite. If this is to be a just society, if we are all forced to pay our taxes, if our constituents must pay taxes, if we must observe the laws of this country, I say that Mr. John Christopher Doyle, who for years-

I note that the time of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) was extended for five minutes. I say this: as long as I am in the Chamber I will never consent to any hon. gentleman opposite speaking beyond his allotted time. They are a discourteous bunch, and ignorant.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: We won't have to worry; you are not here that much.

Hear, hear!
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, the budget speech delivered by the Minister of Finance on March 31, 1977 contains several measures aimed at restoring confidence in society and stimulating economic growth by promoting corporate investments. It provides more assistance to small and medium-sized businesses and to venture enterprises, and thus promotes job creation. The budget provides tax relief for Canadians most affected by the rising cost of living. It also contains other measures aimed at promoting regional growth.
The first matter I would like to deal with, Mr. Speaker, concerns tax relief for individuals. For the first time since taxation year 1972, Canadian workers were entitled to deduct as working expenses 3 per cent of their earnings up to $150. On several occasions in the past, like some of my colleagues no doubt, I urged the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and his predecessor to increase that amount.
The budget provides for a new maximum of $250.
This amount represents a tax reduction for the Canadian worker, but I should have liked a greater increase to cover more of the additional costs for transportation to the place of work, the purchase of tools, books, working outfits and what have you. I trust, Mr. Speaker, that as soon as economic conditions will permit it, we shall look again into this matter, and that we shall not wait four or five years before doing so.
Moreover, income tax cuts have increased from 8 to 9 per cent, as a result of the new fiscal agreements with the provinces. These cuts vary from a $500 maximum to a $200 minimum, and thus favour taxpayers with low incomes. Effective in 1977, the taxpayer will be able to deduct also up to $50 for every dependent child under 18 years of age who is residing in Canada. For instance, the taxpayer with two children who is now entitled to a $350 tax cut, will be able to deduct an additional $100. The current $500 ceiling remains the same, so that this measure will mostly benefit the taxpayers with large families and low incomes. In 1977, with this change millions of Canadians should be able to save a total of $275 million in income tax.

Thanks to those new measures, a great many Canadians will also have a higher personal income. In some cases, they will no longer have to pay any federal income tax; that will be the case for the wage-earner with two dependent children and earning less than $7,360. The same will apply to a family man with four children whose income amounts to $8,295. Of course, many other categories of taxpayers will also benefit from a lower income tax.
Some hon. members of the opposition parties claim that the government should have done more to relieve the taxpayers. But no one has mentioned another decrease in income tax, which will amount to $900 million in 1977, as a result of indexing personal income tax. This plan which was approved by Parliament in 1973 and has been applied since tax year 1974, provides an annual increase in the main exemptions and personal deductions, as well as tax levels which take into account the variations in the cost of living index. As a result, taxpayers do not automatically reach a higher tax bracket merely as a result of inflationary pressures.
For instance, the basic personal exemption, which was $1,706 in 1974, will be $2,270 in 1977. The personal exemption of married couples for the same period increased from $1,492 to $1,990, and finally, the exemption allowed to elderly and disabled persons will now be $1,420 compared to $1,066 in 1974. Maximum exemptions for children increase from $320 and $586 in 1974, to $430 and $780 for the current year. All these changes in exemptions represent an increase of about 33 per cent. In 1976, tax indexing resulted in a $1.25 billion reduction in tax revenue. In another sector involving workers, Mr. Speaker, unemployment insurance premiums in 1977 will decrease by approximately $250 million.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock.

speechtext: Hon. members have just heard the suggestion. Agreed.
[ Translation]

As regards job creation, in the last budget the federal government injects an additional $100 million in the employment program, thus increasing to $660 for this year the appropriation for a comprehensive employment strategy by the government. Under this employment strategy, the new programs Canada Works and Young Canada Works will have
April 21, 1977

a major impact on job creation, but on the whole those are temporary jobs.
Let us be realistic. In order to reduce substantially the number of unemployed, the co-operation of all government levels, private industry and labour unions is required. I for one believe that the private sector is still in a better position to create the largest number of permanent jobs. We must create a favourable climate and in some cases offer incentives so that the private sector can produce at a cost which allows it to be competitive at the import level both on the domestic and the international markets. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, small and medium-sized businesses can play a very important role.
I welcomed the appointment of a Minister of State who would look exclusively after matters relating to small and medium-sized businesses. There are about 400,000 of them in Canada and this sector could play a very important part in creating new jobs. I read with interest the speech delivered on February 19, 1977 by the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand), the Minister responsible for Small Businesses, to the Yellowknife Chamber of Commerce, when he said among other things that he would bring forward amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act in order to make it more useful. This initiative is timely because the last amendments to this act go back to March 12, 1970, and those were only minor amendments.
Under this act, between January 1, 1976 and September 30, 1976, 3,783 loans were granted for a total amount of approximately $53,593,192. The Small Businesses Loans Act took effect in January 1961. From that date until the end of September 1976, a total of $452,453,213 was granted in loans, that is an average of $28 million a year, which means that this act was not fully used, and we should seriously wonder why, Mr. Speaker, because after all, its effects are spread over a period of 16 years.
Small businesses are faced with several problems, but I am going to mention two of them: working capital and management. It is often difficult for small businesses to find outside capital. They have no access to financial and monetary markets because of their size. Very often, banks are reluctant to loan them money either because the extent of their needs exceeds the duration of normal credits or because their financial situation and their profit-earning capacity do not meet the standards which apply to the regular reimbursement of the loan requested.
Mr. Speaker, I urged the Ministers of Finance and Industry, Trade and Commerce on several occasions to improve the existing legislation in order to help small industry. I hope the Minister of State reponsible for Small Businesses will amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, in order to prompt financial institutions such as banks, credit unions and other such institutions to finance small businesses at more favourable conditions than those offered their regular customers and that he will coordinate all the operations of departments and Crown corporations which are in a position to provide services to small businesses.
The Budget-Mr. Clermont
Someone will certainly say, Mr. Speaker, that many financial institutions in the private sector can help finance small businesses and that loan applicants turned down by these institutions can always go to the Federal Business Development Bank, which replaced the Industrial Development Bank in October 1975. The Federal Business Development Bank is a Crown corporation and, according to the mandate it received from the Canadian Parliament, it acts as a last recourse for loans for small businesses in Canada.
In certain sectors, it is even considered superfluous competition. I for one do not believe this to be true. According to the latest information given on February 24, 1977 to the members of the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs by the chairman of the bank, Mr. Richard Murray, it provided financial assistance to 32,300 businesses and its liabilities totalled $1.4 billion. Others will say that its requirements for granting loans are still too strict. It seems that the bank has been more open in the last three or four years, but in my opinion its services are limited since it has only 88 branches in Canada, including 18 in Quebec. This is why it is very important for managers of small businesses to have local access to financing.
The Industrial Development Bank had an advisory management service which was much emphasized in November 1975 by the Federal Business Development Bank, under sections 21, 22 and 23 of the Act. The advisory management services of the bank come under three categories, which are management counselling, management training and information services. As concerns management counselling, the Federal Business Development Bank offers services through consultation with the business service, whose staff includes retired businessmen and businesswomen. In 1976, 3,600 requests were received for these services.
As concerns management training for small businesses, the bank offers seminars. In 1976, 13,000 people took part in such activities. Under its information services, the bank publishes a series of brochures entitled Your business is our business, which deal with various aspects of small business management. Some 472,800 copies were distributed free of charge in 1976.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that during the course of its consultations, the Federal Business Development Bank is only working on the surface considering the number of small businesses.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to discuss another matter, that is the Neighbourhood Improvement Program under which the federal government can offer a wide range of subsidies and loans through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to encourage the upgrading of living conditions in neighbourhoods which otherwise would become unfit for living.
This program aims at encouraging and assisting efforts of municipalities which work in cooperation with residents of these neighbourhoods to improve the physical environment and develop social and recreative services. Implementation of this program is being done through agreements concluded between the government of Canada and each province. The provinces designate municipalities which can be part of that program and municipalities in turn select the neighbourhoods to be

April 21, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Clermont
improved. Within this program, the rehabilitation of existing homes is one of the main objectives considered by the federal government. As soon as a municipality starts implementing its Neighbourhood Improvement Program, local residents become eligible for loans and subsidies which can be granted for repairing and restoring their homes.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to submit two changes to the minister in charge of this program. The first one is that the present $10,000 maximum loan be increased and the second that the present $11,000 adjusted family income maximum be also increased for live-in owners. The reason we should raise these limits is that construction and repair costs are higher than they were, and so are the average wages of the people who could benefit from this program.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with a point which is very important for my area; it has to do with the economic revival of the private sector through the growth and the creation of new manufacturing and processing industries, which will give more job opportunities to the people of this area. It is more than ever a matter of urgency now that the federal government has decided to decentralize its administration in different parts of the country and also due to the lower increase in the number of civil servants.
It is a well-recognized fact that the federal government is a very large employer in the national capital area, although two-thirds of the working population are employed elsewhere. It can be expected that the civil service growth rate will not go unchecked. Here are certain indications to that effect: in 1973, 1974 and 1975, the growth rates in our area were 5.5, 5.6 and 6.8 per cent. The President of the Treasury Board forecasted a 1.3 per cent increase for the whole civil service in 1976, and his forecast for 1977 is 0.06 per cent. The Minister of Public Works of Canada announced that the federal government will not proceed with phases 6 and 7 of its Place du Portage building complex in Hull. We also know that current projections of the local building industry are not very promising.
In a talk to the Commercial and Industrial Development Corp. of Ottawa, NCC Chairman Pierre Juneau outlined the role the NCC might play in the future development and diversification of the private economic structure in the area, while coordinating its efforts with all groups in the area.
My colleague from Hull, Dr. Gaston Isabelle, and myself recently made representations to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard), to the effect that the possibility should be considered of designating a special area that part of the Quebec side of the Ottawa area not currently included in such an area. In this way, existing companies wishing to expand and new companies wishing to locate here could receive both capital investment grants and make job grants. It will be remembered that when the new development agreement was signed between Canada and the province of Quebec on March 15, 1974, the Montreal-Hull corridor was not included. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I express the hope that everyone will cooperate for a new economic departure for our area.

AFTER RECESS
