Mr. Speaker, I take part in this budget debate with a speech that has been ready for some time. I would like to begin by referring to write-ins which I received during December and January from the beef industry in my constituency. This was rather an extraordinary set of letters. The number of individual post offices that mailed to me was surprising for this kind of write-in. It was an indication of the extreme concern felt by that branch of Canadian agriculture. They were protesting the low price of beef produced in Canada. They were protesting the volume of imports from other nations around the world that seemed to have very free access into this country.
The thing that struck me is that I have letters from Armstrong, Enderby, Grindrod, Lumby, Salmon Arm, Sicamous and Vernon on the Okanagan side. I also have letters from Brisco, Cranbrook, Elko, Fairmont Hot Springs, Fernie, Fort Steele, Golden, Grasmere, Harrogate, Invermere, Jaffray, Kimberley, Marysville, Sparwood, Spillimacheen, Ta Ta Creek, Wardner and Wycliffe on the Kootenay side. There are some time honoured names there and some historic names. There are some large communities and some small communities. In each there are individuals who were involved and still are involved in the beef industry.
The point I would like to make tonight is that that is an industry that traditionally should be an employer. It is an industry that is productive. It is an industry that is based on Canadian resources of land, grass and grain. It is an industry that is in desperate trouble at the present time. It is an industry that is, by and large, managed by self-employed. It should be an employer, particularly of young people and young people without too much skill. In the past it has been an employer of young people without too much education. But if you are going to be really successful in that industry now in terms of owning and managing, it requires a high degree of education and of skill. It should still, however, have room for people who like to work for a few years. It should have room for people who like to work outdoors and who may not have much education but who would be willing to work hard in

April 21, 1977

conditions that are sometimes difficult, but certainly exhilarating.
There is not an operation from this list of communities that is not getting along now with as few people as it possibly can. In many cases the operation has probably been reduced to family members and family members only, because of the difficulties of obtaining help, the cost of it, and because of all of the other crises and costs that beset that industry in a time when prices have reached lows that have not been since the depression years.
The budget promises very little to my province. It does allocate another $100 million to the Canada Works Program. That program was started this year, and that leaves me wondering about the competence of the government, about its direction and about the reason the Local Initiatives Program, which started out for local initiatives, was turned into a program for direct incentive job creation and was continued with a new name. It has been dressed up, but it will not be any more significant in attacking the problem of unemployment.
Projects under that program may have been good ideas when they started out, and I suspect they originated from the very successful centennial projects which were embarked upon in 1967. Under that program communities raised funds which were matched by the government, and a good many interesting things were done in that exciting year across Canada. That program was drawn up to meet a set of expectations. It had to be temporary, unplanned, spontaneous and local, and this produced some very interesting projects, particularly in my province, so interesting that in many ways they became a minor scandal. It was felt by a good portion of the population that public funds should not be handed out quite as indiscriminately as they were under that program.
Efforts were made to bring a little more inspection to the program. A scheme was devised by the minister then responsible to have members of parliament check the projects or set up constituency advisory groups to do that. That is a part of the policy with which I did not agree because it forced members of parliament, particularly opposition members, to be a party to the crime. It made hon. members on this side of the House, and I suppose hon. members opposite, part of a selection process, which would not have been necessary if the program had been redesigned.
There was another set of requirements as well because it was not desirable to build up a dependency, to have continuity, or to have too much organization. Certainly the one thing the program lacked most of all was co-ordination with existing agencies in the field, and particularly with government at the municipal, school board, parks board, or hospital board levels.
For two years I examined the projects which came to my constituency. Then in frustration a year ago I set up a constituency advisory group for the first time. I spent many hours last summer in my far flung constituency putting the group together, and eventually ten people met and helped to divide up the allocation.
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
I knew the allocation was going to be far less than the allocation of the previous year, and yet as I drove through the constituency last summer with my car radio on, I heard a flood of expensive advertizing urging people to apply. As I expected, when the first allocation came out we had only $459,000 to spread among almost as many applications as we had had the previous year when there was over $1 million to distribute. The constituency advisory group met, and I felt it did a good job with the limited amount it had. It had to make some rather stern decisions and impose a cut-off line.
In spite of one's co-operation, one never gets the job of sending out good news to the constituency. That is done by the program office. My job is to telephone the bad news to those who do not succeed. The telephone began to ring, and I replied to the callers that I would not overrule my constituency advisory group and that I would abide by its decision because I had set up the group to decide for me what I had been deciding during the previous two years. I more or less rode out that storm. Then to my surprise a second allocation of $683,000 was made, one and one half times the original allocation. We had something like four or five days in which to re-examine the applications which had been considered by the constituency advisory group.
There was no hope of calling that group back together. The people who worked with that group must have wondered why they had bothered in the first place because they eventually learned that the field worker, in consultation with me, divided up one and one half times as much money as they had divided up previously.
As we worked on that we heard that something new was in the works and that we were going to have a Canada Works Program. According to some of the initial advertising, the program in some ways would be an improvement over the Local Initiatives Program because we were told it would have continuity, it would be year round, there would not be drastic cut-off dates, it would be possible to get a project under way and there would not be as much difficulty finishing it within a hopeless deadline. We were told there would be the possibility of working in better weather than the weather we find in the dead of winter. We hoped that something better would come.
I honestly believed that there would be some breathing time and that the department would take about a year to re-think seriously what it was doing when it was turning local initiatives into job creation. I hoped that if it was serious about job creation, it might consider other ways of bringing it about.
It is no wonder that the Canadian Manufacturers Association in a brief just the other day had very little good to say about Canada Works or Local Initiatives. Canadian manufacturers should be the job creators at the present time. In far too many cases they are not because of various government restrictions. I am sure the people from the cattle industry who sent the mail-ins are not too happy about what has come about because although Canada Works is a re-named program, it has not changed.
Again there was a remarkable advertising program being broadcast. Even as manpower resources were strained to the

April 21, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
limit to spread that second LIP allocation around, and even before the application forms were out and before anyone knew what was really happening, there were cheerful voices on the radio. I listened to them again as I drove around my constituency. They were telling people to apply because there was lots of money available. They hinted that the amounts were far larger than they had been under the Local Initiatives Program. Colourful newspaper advertisements told people to call their municipal government and ask for a new firehall. We know how much it would cost to build a new firehall these days; yet it was suggested that the program would pretty well cover the cost.
Not surprisingly, in my constituency alone that advertising campaign drew applications the cost of which totalled $1,963,303. There is one thing about the statistics I am about to give; they are marvellously metric. When the allocation came it was one tenth of that amount, $190,000. A part of that was designated for Indian reservations, so the portion for the rest of the constituency was reduced by $46,000. I was curious, so I checked to find out how much the advertising for that program in my constituency cost. Marvellously metric again, over $19,000 was paid for advertising. That amount certainly would have helped to fund another application, and it would not have needed to be spent at all because I am sure word of mouth would have brought in more than enough applications to use the $190,000 which was allocated.
I suppose it is one form of restraint. But it should be investigated by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) who spoke just prior to my entry into this debate, because if ever there was an example of false or misleading advertising, it is what the $19,000 bought. I doubt whether the minister, in his carefully read statement, announced that he was investigating the Manpower department for misleading advertising, but it might have been a good idea.
I raised some questions at the time on the distribution of allocations in B.C. I raised the question about the failure of the special small program to pay for material costs to touch British Columbia at all. I have one rule of thumb for LIP, that is, that I do not return any money allocated to my constituency. In the end one is forced into the position of agreeing to some rather dubious projects at times, but few programs that emanate from Ottawa reach across the Rockies into B.C. and I would be remiss in my duty as a member from that province if I returned funds to be disbursed somewhere else. But I raised questions about the formula that was used, both for that material cost program and for the allocations themselves, because it was surprising that the larger allocations went entirely to Liberal ridings.
Now we have received a second allocation, and again a letter has just arrived from the minister setting out the complications of his formula and announcing that a new allocation has been found. Would you believe that of the seven largest ones, six are to Liberal constituencies? The surprising thing about that is

that the second allocation in every one of those six constituencies is larger than the first one, whereas when you come down to the other constituencies-which by and large are NDP and Conservative-the second allocation is sometimes only one quarter of what the first one was, The formula which did not work very well before is even more invidious this time and leaves one wondering whether the aim is to do anything about unemployment, or whether the aim is rather to attempt to ensure the return to parliament of a few members on that side of the House in the next election, which cannot come too soon.
So I found myself frustrated again when another set of applications came in. They received unfunded priority of some 200 per cent, but the share for Okanagan-Kootenay in the renewed allocation is only $122,000. My constituency divides neatly into two halves, so it amounts to only $61,000 on each side. It will not begin to cover even the priority applications. There will have to be one or two choices made out of all those that came in through the advertising program, and not too much will be done to accomplish anything to ease the unemployment in the Okanagan Valley, with respect to which the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) joined me in telling you is very high. The mysterious formula that is used has something to do with the cost of houses and with annual incomes back in 1971 as well as with the present rate of unemployment.
I suggest to the minister that he accept the cardinal rule that when his civil servants come to him with a formula that allocates the bulk load of the money to Liberal ridings, he send them back and tell them to remake the formula. Unless of course he is the person who has ordered them to come up with such a formula, and one suspects that is the explanation for anything that happens twice in a row. It is even more scandalous the second time around than it was the first time.
I see my time is running out, Mr. Speaker, but let me say that I am convinced that if the government wants to do something about unemployment, it should do it through policies and through reduced taxation. It should do it as much as possible through the establishment of an economic climate which will allow at least the continuation of private business if not its expansion. If those fail, then surely to goodness there are enough government institutions at the federal level to provide some employment, with the Armed Forces, for example, and in other areas such as in scientific and medical research, which has been starved for too long, and with the Canada Council, because when the federal government eases off-and that seems to be the main area to which restraint is applied-then we know that highly qualified, young, intelligent and able people are forced to move down the employment ladder and bump other people out of jobs, who then move even farther down and compete with those beneath them, so that in the end we have a pool of unemployed at the bottom whom it is very difficult to help. Certainly nothing very constructive can be done for them through programs such as LIP.
Here at least it seems to me that if the government were really interested in doing something about unemployment, it could work at the municipal level of government and dispense
April 21, 1977

money there, as used to be true with the winter works program which tackled the problem of inflation in a far more sensible way than anything we have seen in the last ten years. At least there was a hope in this program for some kind of supervision, some sort of expertise. Now when there are municipalities, cities, towns and regional districts with their engineers and planners, with their five year programs, the efforts that the federal government makes to cure unemployment should be made at that level in a co-ordinated and co-operative manner. You can imagine what it does to a municipal council that is working under the kind of restraint that is imposed upon it and that has a five year plan, when the federal government overrides it and inserts advertisements in local papers saying, "Call up your municipal council and tell them you want a new fire hall".
Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but the time allotted to him has expired.
Mr. Speaker, this budget has been called a Conservative budget.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Not by a Conservative, it hasn't.

Members on my right say it is not. I say it is the kind of budget that that darling of the Chatham Chamber of Commerce, D'Arcy McKeough, brought down a few nights ago. Here is how he described the Liberal government's budget, and 1 quote: "Honest medicine that will lead to a safer and fairer economic future for our wage earners and our unemployed". No one can accuse D'Arcy McKeough of not being the darling of the Conservative set.
I am not surprised that the Tories are not puffing out their chests and taking credit for this budget, but if they were to be at least as honest as D'Arcy, they would admit that it is the kind of budget that a federal Tory government would have brought in because it reflects the reality of a tired, unimaginative and helpless government unable to take charge of the economy and give the kind of leadership necessary to set about the task of solving our economic and social problems.
Three particular characteristics about this budget emerge which reinforce the concept of the Liberal ship of state rudderless and awash in a sea of economic uncertainty. The first one of these characteristics is the traditional approach of fighting inflation on the backs of the unemployed.
Let us go back to the year when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office. In 1968 the unemployment rate was 4.8 per cent and the inflation rate was 4 per cent. By 1970 unemployment had reached 5 per cent and the inflation rate was 5.6 per cent. It was then that the Prime Minister began his fight with inflation-one would wish that he had not-and he vowed that he would defeat inflation even if the unemployment rate rose above 6 per cent.
Unemployment was not only used ruthlessly against inflation, but also against a trend that the federal Liberals and
The Budget-Mr. Rodriguez
their corporate friends were finding ominous. Between 1964 and 1970, labour's share of the national income had been rising in comparison to the corporate share. As a matter of fact by 1970 labour's share of the national income had reached 72.8 per cent.
The government decided that this trend had to be stopped and one of the most efficient ways of taking income away from labour is to reduce the demand for it, in other words, create unemployment. In effect the government would be killing two birds with one stone-fighting inflation and controlling wages.
The government was successful. Labour's share of the national income fell from 72.8 per cent in 1970 to 67 per cent in the first half of 1974. Unemployment in the same period had risen to 6.8 per cent. There was one fly in the ointment; the inflation rate had reached double digits and labour, which had been locked into two and three-year contracts during this period, was starting to negotiate catch-up agreements and COLA clauses. As a result, by mid 1975 labour's share of the national income had started to rise again and reached 70.8 per cent, still a long way behind the position it had attained in 1970, but in the government's and the private sector's view, too high for profit comfort.
The government again decided that labour was getting too fat at the expense of the business sector which was crying the blues that its profits were lower than the super-profit days of the early 1970's. But how was the government going to put labour in its place this time? It could no longer stand up and deliberately admit setting out to create unemployment-which by this time was pushing 7 per cent. The Canadian public would just not accept the arrogance of a Prime Minister who promised massive unemployment "to fight inflation." Instead the government decided to control wages when it brought in the AIB program after the 1974 federal election in which the Liberal party opposed wage controls.
By the end of last year inflation was 7.5 per cent, but the most recent increase in the cost of living of 1 per cent extrapolates to double digit inflation for this year. The army of unemployed now has 944,000 reluctant volunteers and is growing daily. It is something to think about when the Treasurer of Ontario tells us that Ontario residents have to live with 5 per cent unemployment-that 200,000 people out of work is considered full employment in the province of Ontario. Meanwhile, to date the AIB has rolled back corporate profits by $13 million while wages of Canadian workers have been rolled back $300 million.
It is quite evident from this budget that we should not hold our collective breaths for the "Big Mac Attack" on the most serious problem facing Canada at the moment-unemployment. The AIB program is kept in force and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has made it clear in his budget speech that the traditional and disastrous approach is still being taken. He said:
Our goals are clear. Our first objective must be to maintain the underlying trend to lower inflation.
The second characteristic of this budget which indicates a bankruptcy of ideas on the part of the government in dealing

April 21, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Rodriguez
with the Canadian economy is the clear admission by the Minister of Finance that we do not control our economic destiny.
My colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman), put the situation in its proper perspective when he said the other day that the Canadian government decided that it would do nothing about the economic problems facing the country but wait for the American cavalry to come charging over the hill. Well, Mr. Speaker, we have been waiting and waiting, and listening for the trumpet call of approaching cavalry, but there is nothing so far, only a worsening economic plight in Canada.
The Minister of Finance made it clear in his budget speech that we are going to go on waiting. He said:
... with renewed growth in our economic trading partners, we can expect further improvements in our trade balance.
While we are waiting for help to arrive from south of the border we have at least one million people unemployed and inflation running at over 7.5 per cent, factories operating at 80 per cent capacity, a Prime Minister who suggests to our unemployed youth that they should work in other countries and, above all, a pontificating Minister of Finance who in his budget speech said:
What is required is that we accept the inevitable impact of these price increases upon our living standards, turn to substitutes where we can and reduce our demands for the higher priced goods to the extent possible. Above all we must avoid a renewed, self-defeating scramble for higher incomes.
The next time 1 go to Newfoundland, Cape Breton or northern New Brunswick, and when I am in my riding of Nickel Belt speaking with the unemployed, I will tell them that the Minister of Finance has said they must give up their "higher-priced goods".
The fact of the matter is that there is no national economic planning on the part of the government and, as a result, the country continues to be developed as a resource based economy-a situation which any self-respecting industrialized nation would never permit. The major part of our trading relationship with Japan is a microcosm of Canada's relationship with the industrialized nations of the world. For instance, 96 per cent of all our exports to Japan are raw materials, and 95 per cent of all our imports from Japan are finished products-cars, cameras, electronic equipment, etc.
No wonder the Japanese are willing to invest in developing Canadian resources. It is because they know that the jobs are not in the extraction of the resources from the ground but rather in the finishing of these resources to final products.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, what are we up to in Canada? We not only invite foreign investors to exploit our resources but we also pay them to explore for those resources, and pay them again when those resources have been ripped out. We pay them depreciation allowances and we even allow them to defer their taxes to the people of Canada. No, Mr. Speaker, there is no rape in this process because we have consented to the act and, moreover, this government enjoys it.

Contrary to popular corporate belief, the government, selected to lead and make policy in and for the country, must intervene purposefully and deliberately in planning the development of the economy of Canada. There is a need for a natural resources policy with public ownership of the energy and non-renewable sectors. There is definite need for transportation and communications policies, to move not only products but also to keep our citizens in touch, no matter in which end of Canada they live.
This leads me to comment on the third aspect of this budget which clearly indicates to many that the government has neither the necessary comprehension of the seriousness of the problem facing us, nor the creative imagination necessary to attack it.
I think it was appropriate that the Prime Minister spent some of his Easter recess at Disneyland. He seems to have fitted in well with Mickey Mouse, Minnie Mouse, and Pluto. But he missed the point completely. I suppose there was much he could have learned at Disneyland in terms of creative imagination, from Walt Disney.
But the third aspect is the one which places a great deal of trust in the corporate sector to provide the necessary growth in the economy. The government, in order to display its trust, handed over $1.2 billion in tax concessions to corporate and investor groups. One cannot help but wonder out loud at the need for this priming when we note that Canadian industry is already operating at as much as 20 per cent below capacity. Furthermore, the dividend tax credit would permit someone with no other source of income to make up to $23,750 in dividends without paying one cent in tax. Also, the treatment of stock options as a capital gain would certainly allow certain companies to provide their executives with remuneration on which they would pay only half the normal tax. But will this priming of the private sector really help us to solve our unemployment problem? Let us look at the experience of the last decade or so.
From January, 1961, to December, 1963, we had double depreciation rates in the first year for investment in designated surplus manpower areas or for new products. The total amount of depreciation was unchanged. From June, 1961, to March, 1964, we saw a 50 per cent increase in the depreciation rate in the first year for investment in the form of re-equipment and modernization. This was additional to the total amount of depreciation. From June, 1963, to March, 1967, we had a straight line depreciation rate for machinery and equipment expenditures, which had previously been depreciated at 20 per cent on a declining balance, and a 20 per cent straight line depreciation rate for building expenditures, by manufacturing and processing industry. This was subject to Canadian ownership conditions. From June, 1963, to March, 1967, we saw a three-year tax exemption on income from new manufacturing and processing business in designated areas. From April, 1967, to March, 1971, we saw tax free area development program grants, to replace the three-year tax exemption which expired
April 21, 1977

at the end of March, 1967, a 20 per cent straight line depreciation rate for buildings and a 50 per cent rate for machinery and equipment in those designated areas.
Between December, 1970, and March, 1972, the government instituted valuation at 115 per cent of cost, for depreciation purposes, of building, machinery and equipment expenditures by manufacturing and processing industry. Beginning in May, 1972-this program is still in effect-the government instituted 50 per cent straight line depreciation of machinery and equipment expenditures by manufacturing and processing business. In January, 1973-again this program is in force today-the government instituted a reduction in the top tax rate for manufacturing and processing industry, from 50 per cent to 40 per cent. Between May, 1974, and April, 1975, the government allowed an exemption on manufacturing and processing profits from the 10 per cent surtax on corporate tax. That provision applies only to the period mentioned. In June, 1975, the government instituted the investment tax credit, amounting to 5 per cent of the cost of new buildings, machinery, and equipment for use in manufacturing and processing. This can be carried forward for five years.
Billions upon billions of dollars, Mr. Speaker, have been poured into the private sector during the past dozen years. How come, then, that we have an unemployment problem equal to depression year proportions? The answer is that the private sector has failed to satisfy our employment needs in Canada. All the same, the present Minister of Finance is giving that private sector another $1.2 billion. Perhaps the minister and the Prime Minister have been watching too many insurance company advertisements about freeing enterprise and have decided to let the vulture out of the cage.
All this extra money going to the private sector will only fatten profits, because who in his right mind would invest when they are not using the plant and equipment they already have? For example, in the last quarter of 1976 the food and beverage industry was operating at 85 per cent of capacity; the rubber and plastics industry at 70.4 per cent; leather at 62.1 per cent; textiles at 83.6 per cent; wood at 75.5 per cent; furniture and fixtures at 70.3 per cent; paper and allied industries at 79.3 per cent; primary metals at 65.8 per cent; metal fabricating at 80.8 per cent; and electrical products at 79.5 per cent.
The finance minister even admitted in his speech that slack demand in 1976 led to a significant fall in profit margins. If demand is so slight that we have falling profit margins, how will we convince people to invest? It sounds like a good trick, but I don't think it is going to work.
Even Roy Phillips, executive director of the Canadian Manufacturer's Association, admitted recently that "Last year
206,000	workers in manufacturing industries saw their jobs disappear." That is 10 per cent of our manufacturing labour force.
Canadians in various sectors of the economy are light years apart in their reactions to the budget. Mr. Sam Hughes, executive director of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce,
The Budget-Mr. Rodriguez
said of the budget, "We're grinning from ear to ear." And well he might be grinning.
On the other hand Paul Lepage of the New Brunswick Federation of Labour said, "This budget is going to grind our people down."
Mr. William Daniel of Shell Canada said, "I have to say that it's a business oriented budget." On the other hand Terry Meagher of the Ontario Federation of Labour said, "I can't believe that the government can be that heartless, that out of touch with reality."
There is a considerable difference between those two positions, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps that difference is there because labour leaders are closer to our 1 million unemployed than are corporation presidents. Maybe they notice that a 9 per cent unemployment rate means drastic effects on the lives of real people. They are unlike the writers for the Financial Post who blithely point out that the American economy did not disintegrate when the Americans had a 9 per cent unemployment rate. Is that how far we must go before this government does something for our employed? Must the economy disintegrate before it becomes important that our young people cannot find work and 20 per cent of our population lives in poverty?
There are short-term and long-term approaches to dealing with unemployment. I have tried to hammer my points home for at least six months. I have talked about the long-term approach involving national economic planning and government participation in the economy, and have indicated what ought to be done. I am certainly quick to agree that government spending can cause inflation, but it depends on how the money is spent. How can a government's deficit spending be inflationary when the economy is not operating at full capacity?
It is an indictment of any government that a so-called, responsible minister-in this case the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen)-should rise to his feet in parliament and say that we cannot afford an employment program and that we are better off wasting the money spent on training people for jobs that are not there. We ought to look at some of the other costs of high unemployment. If we could reduce by 100,000 the number of unemployed, we could save $480 million paid out in unemployment insurance alone. And what about savings in welfare expenditures, and other social services expenditures? Has anyone considered the number of tax dollars the country loses because the unemployed are not earning decent wages?
Also, what about the cost of unemployment in human terms? Studies done in other countries where unemployment rates are high show that suicide rates among the unemployed are higher than the national average. The incidence of severe depression among the unemployed is greater. One finds that, owing to depression, the incidence of brutalization of children is greater among the unemployed than among the general population. Therefore please do not say that we cannot afford a decent employment program. The fact is that we cannot afford not to have a decent employment program.

April 21, 1977
The Budget-Miss Begin
It makes me even more sick when I remember that in 1971-72, when the unemployment rate was 6.4 per cent, the federal government announced direct job creation expenditures of $600 million. Yet in 1977-78, when it is forecast that unemployment will rise to over 8 per cent, the government will spend only $350 million in direct job creation programs. But the government says we do not have to worry, because private enterprise is going to pick up the slack.
Order please.
I have heard that before. I heard that last year, from the Minister of Manpower and Immigration.
Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but must inform him that his allotted time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not swamp my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), with compliments but I must tell the House how much I admire that man for the courage he showed in refusing to talk rubbish to the people of Canada- and here I refer to the speech we have just heard from the honourable member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez)-to humbug them, as we say in Quebec, at a time when the treasury cannot afford expenditures for which it has no money.
The Minister of Finance-and at times the truth hurts deeply-the Minister of Finance, after having applied for more than a year the most innovative program in any industrialized country to create jobs, quickly and flexibly, which unfortunately are rather unstable, namely the LIP type of jobs, had to give private industry incentives to give it new stimulation and enable it, in turn, to assume its share of responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is all too easy to address stirring words to the people when one has few real governmental responsibilities, as is the case of the previous speaker. Some of the budgetary measures fall under two divisions of my department, that is customs and excise, under taxation. I would like to say a few words about them. There will be no earthshaking statements. I am not going to quote the Bible, but those measures come very close to the daily life of Canadians and that is what is important to me. This is no time for great undertakings and stirring rhetoric.
For instance, lower tariffs on a wide variety of consumer goods will apply for another year. Those lower rates were passed in 1973 to slow down inflationary pressures. Materials used directly for religious, educational and medical purposes will also be duty-free.
We took protectionist measures-and I am directly concerned because of my responsibility as a minister-by establishing a higher tariff to help sugar refiners, electric fixture producers and heavy machinery and related equipment manufacturers who had some trouble before because of the competition of imported goods.

I am not always sure that we opt for the best long-term solution when we take protectionist measures which keep sick industries artificially alive when surgery alone could work out miracles, namely industries which should be converted into other areas of the manufacturing process. Of course, I am not talking here about the people I have just mentioned who receive tariff help in the March 31 budget. I think it is essential to ensure self-sufficiency at any price, or at least some freedom of action and negotiation for a country like Canada in areas such as food production and energy.
What shocks me is the poor situation of Quebecers. As a matter of fact, the industrial structure of Quebec could be summed up not as "La belle province" but rather as "the province of textile and footwear industry". The dilemma faced by the government is that all of a sudden it has its back against the wall because some plants are going to close down at a time when inflation is combined with unemployment, when we do not have any quick alternative program to transform these non competitive jobs into stable and permanent jobs.
I realize that such a statement is not regarded as "political" but it will b? still less so to conceal the truth and face the political judgment of those who will follow us if we have refused to take up the challenge offered in particular by Quebec, a little by Toronto and, generally, by the eastern half the country.
That might be the very nature of Canada which has no other market than its sparse 22 million population as opposed to the natural and huge market of the country to the south which does not hesitate to overprotect itself when it decides to do so. It might also be that we were short of hands while putting all our hearts and minds to unify this threatened country, in explaining Quebecers to other Canadians, which is relatively easy to do, and in repatriating Canada in Quebecers' minds with a new emotion, which is something more difficult, and trying at the same time to lead the economy through a hard period when unemployment runs ahead of inflation.
I could not help making this digression, Mr. Speaker, because I would like to be sure that Canadians and their leaders on all side of the House are aware of our precarious position as a commercial partner as well as the urgency of taking, I believe, a gradual approach towards the liberalization of exchanges. To return now to the Department of Revenue which administers excise tax legislation, I would like to explain the impact that the amendments to this legislation which were proposed in the budget might have on the taxpayer.
First, let us talk about the exemptions for the disabled. The Excise Tax Act provides for exemptions for some goods and services to ease the movement of the disabled. It is now proposed to add wheel chair lifts to that list and to authorize the governor in council to exempt some other items of assistance to the disabled. This is in reply to many requests by individuals or associations and by members from this side of the House among others; but we had to reject them because the act did not allow us to agree to their requests.

The fact that we will now get authorization from the governor in council to do so will allow us to meet the needs of Canadians much more rapidly. Moreover, institutions or public agencies using buses or small vans for the sole purpose of moving the handicapped will no longer have to pay the tax on these vehicles, provided they are equipped to move the handicapped and designed in such a way that they can eventually move 12 passengers or more.
In co-operation with the Metric Commission and to encourage people to go metric by July 1, 1981, the sales tax will apply on only half the value of the new metric scales. The scales, however, must be used to weigh goods of 100 kilos or less in retail sales. Assistance is also provided for those who would like to alter good existing scales and they will not have to pay the tax when purchasing the necessary parts for that alteration.
In 1974, it was decided that a tax exemption would be granted on small buses. Since then, a tax exemption is granted for motor vehicles designed to carry 12 passengers or more. It is now suggested that two conditions will be required to be allowed that exemption. First, the vehicles must be designed and permanently equipped to carry 12 passengers or more, but they must also be used exclusively to carry passengers. For example, the case of a hotel or motel owner providing his customers with a transport service to the airport would come under the definitions of my department. The scope of that new exemption has been extended to include rail-free train systems which are sometimes found in large parks for tourist attractions and so on.
Another proposal with which my department is involved is aimed at small manufacturers. It will no longer be necessary to make sales exclusively to consumers or users.

As soon as the budget provisions are passed, I intend to raise from $3,000 to $10,000 the ceiling on the sales of small manufacturers. In addition, I propose to designate craftsmen as a separate class of small manufacturers, no matter the volume of their sales. After consulting the people concerned, I suggest that craftsmen be obliged to manufacture or produce personally craftsmanship items as prescribed by regulations, which will reflect a certain aspect of the Canadian culture or heritage. Mr. Speaker, I wish to indicate briefly that we apply measures to assist average income Canadians, that is to say ordinary people. For instance, taxpayers will be able to claim

an additional credit of $50 for every dependent under 18 who is a Canadian resident. Moreover, the ceiling on the 3 per cent deduction for expenses relating to employment, without receipt, will go up from $150 to $250. Mr. Speaker, I will now conclude my remarks by emphasizing how important I consider the future introduction by this government of a guaranteed annual income, whether in the form of a negative tax or otherwise.
I would therefore like to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that I am well aware that my department is a service department and that it collects the $37 billion which will then be spent by my colleagues for programs aimed at Canadians. As I said earlier, I hope that one of the expenditures for which 1 will one day have the privilege of voting as a member of the Privy Council will be the implementation of a guaranteed annual income in one form or another, probably under a phased-in program. I know that in recent years, we have sometimes been forced to take action similar to that favoured in impassioned speeches, like that of the previous speaker. I hope that such adventures will not force us to abandon that in which the Liberal government believes and of which it reaffirms the importance, that is a guaranteed annual income for all Canadians. As Minister of National Revenue, I will make every effort to ensure that every fraction of every penny collected from Canadian taxpayers for the public treasury will be spent for programs corresponding to their concept of a happy country.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the competition for time I shall not be very lengthy tonight since I wish to give other members an opportunity to take part in the debate. My colleagues have already brought to light some of the shortcomings in the budget but I should like to bring to the attention of the House areas in which I am particularly interested since they affect my constituency.
The first of these is in respect to small businessmen's loans and assistance to small business people across Canada. For some time I have protested regarding the Small Business Loans Act, pointing out that there are really no teeth in the legislation. Consequently it is difficult if not impossible for a businessman to secure a small business loan at preferred rates. On March 28 I asked the minister what plans he had to upgrade the position of the small businessmen, bearing in mind that their operations are particularly affected by the present slack in our economy. The Minister of State (Small Businesses) (Mr. Marchand) replied that the act was coming up for amendment at the end of June and that he would be proposing substantial amendments which would made it a much more effective piece of legislation.
I would like to suggest that action be taken to put teeth into the act or make whatever other changes might be necessary to make it easier for a small businessman to secure these loans. Over the past months several cases have been brought to my attention in which local bankers have approved applications for loans, but when these applications reached the head office they were turned down. The reason they were turned down is that at the present time there is more incentive for a bank to lend money at a higher rate of interest than to make loans which are guaranteed under the provisions of the Small Business Loans Act.
Many business people are wondering what good the Small Business Loans Act is when they find they cannot take advantage of its provisions. I have in hand a case which illustrates this situation. To begin, I would like to read, in part, from a letter received by one of my constituents from the Eastern Ontario Region of the Bank of Montreal. It states:
As you are aware, the intent of the Small Business Loans Act is to make available to small businesses, through provisions of a government guarantee, loans which might otherwise not be available. The bank has granted in the past, and continues to grant, business improvement loans in instances where the applicant qualifies and cannot reasonably be accommodated under one of its own programs.
The current interest rate on loans made under the act is considerably below the current market rate for similar loans without the government guarantee. Since loan rates under the act are not subsidized by the government in any way, we are naturally very selective in granting these loans under present market conditions unless our assessment of the risk indicates that the government guarantee is essential. In your own case, we do not consider it is necessary to call upon the government to support your requirements by provision of its guarantee and we are pleased to consider your needs on the basis of your own credit worthiness.
As you can imagine, Mr. Speaker, my constituent was not very encouraged to learn that even though he had a good credit rating, or, indeed, because of it, he could not qualify for a small business loan guaranteed by the government. The

individual in question did write to the minister regarding this and I am sure the matter has been brought to the minister's attention.
Getting down to actual specifics, the individual in question was requiring financing of approximately $50,000. He had no debts against his business and has owned and operated the business since 1950. There were no mortgages on his property and he was initially endorsed for a small business loan at the rate of 9'A per cent interest. The bank, however, determined that it would not give him such a loan and suggested instead a 10-year term loan at a rate of 1094 per cent which would be subject to interest fluctuations.
I am sure it is obvious that something must be done in respect to this matter and I certainly urge the government and the minister to take those steps which are necessary to assist the small business people of our country. Well over half the labour force of Canada is employed in small business, and we certainly need more provisions in the budget which would give direct assistance to the small businessman. Failing this, I urge the minister to bring forth strong amendments to the Small Business Loans Act at the earliest possible date. In all fairness I must state that the minister in charge of the legislation has been co-operative and understanding. He is new in his position and I am sure that as time goes on he will carry out the long overdue measures which are needed to update this act. These loans are not as popular as they used to be. Not many are being taken out.
I believe the banking community of Canada, bearing in mind the success which the banks have enjoyed, ought to give more consideration to the small business community because any weakening of the small business community in Canada will quickly lead to trouble in many quarters. This is a consideration which the government should weigh carefully, because wise decisions here could benefit the economy not only of Ontario but Canada generally.
Another area which I should like to discuss concerns the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. On April 1 I questioned the minister regarding the status of the renewal of the ARDA agreement. I am sure that many other members have received representations from municipalities which are concerned that the ARDA agreement with the province of Ontario expired at the end of last month. I was assured that negotiations were going on and that they should be concluded shortly. In his answer to me the minister indicated that there was really no delay as many projects already had money allocated to them and would be carried on. The problem, however, is that until the agreement is renewed, new projects cannot be initiated. It is my understanding that the province of Ontario signed this agreement and that it has been in Ottawa for almost a month awaiting the minister's signature.
This is the time of year when many new ventures under ARDA should be getting under way. With the approach of spring which our beautiful weather currently indicates is now every day we lose is of serious consequence. As I say,
April 21, 1977

the province of Ontario has signed the agreement and the minister has had it for almost a month. 1 do not understand why some action has not been taken to expedite a matter of great importance to rural communities in Ontario, and 1 urge the minister to make all haste.
I am sure that many individuals have benefited from another department, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. However, I would suggest that the minister consider amending the formula whereby areas qualify for DREE funding. I urge the government to consider extending the area to which DREE applies to take in the counties of Victoria and Haliburton which I represent. In the northern part of my riding particularly the work force is geared to a large extent to tourism, and thus seasonal employment is a major factor. Should DREE assistance be available, I know it would be a great stimulus to the local economy and I trust that my suggestion will be taken into consideration.
In regard to the formula which is used, I have questioned what I thought were the officials in charge of DREE and I can truthfully say that I have never been given the exact formula under which areas are considered for DREE assistance. What the formula is, I do not know, but it should be broadened. 1 think I must say in fairness to our entire economy across Canada that too many areas are being deprived of DREE grants and loans. I think just giving a few chosen areas assistance is neglecting municipalities which, probably by a very fine line, because of the composition of their population, such as having many retired people in the area, or for one reason or another, fail to qualify under the formula.
I should also like to mention that 1 have been receiving a lot of correspondence, not just from my riding but from many places across the province, in connection with a letter circulated by the Canadian government office of tourism here in Ottawa. As I have mentioned, a good part of the economy of my riding is dependent upon the tourist trade, and thus I think one can understand the concern of many individuals in my area about this particular letter which was sent out by the director of marketing of the Canadian office of tourism. This letter was sent to many American fishermen, and it expounded the benefits derived from fishing in Canada. However, it goes on to indicate that the choice of fishing in Canada is almost boundless, and states that Canada offers the fisherman such a vast choice that it is hard to decide where to go. Then at that point the letter takes a specific turn and says:
Let me make a suggestion ...
The letter then goes on for the next page and a half to list the greatness and attraction of fishing in the province of Quebec and suggests that recipients send for a free information kit. Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not for a moment denigrating the quality or attraction of the province of Quebec for the fishermen of America. I know that our neighbour to the east, as well as other provinces, have great and varied attractions for the American tourist, and I trust that many visitors will make use of those facilities. However, I do protest the fact that one particular province or region was given pre-eminence in a government publication which supposedly promotes tourism

for all Canada. I suggest that the action taken by the federal government's office of tourism only further irritates the problems existing between various regions of this great country.
In this connection I have a letter from the Haliburton Highlands Chamber of Commerce, as well as a photostat of the letter sent out by the office of tourism. I know many other members have received complaints about this matter, and I think it only fair to the rest of Canada that some measures be taken to correct what I feel is a bias against a tourist industry which is to be enjoyed and wants to be enjoyed from coast to coast. In closing, I urge the government to give consideration to some of the matters I have raised and to initiate legislation that will permit the economies and labour force of all areas of Canada to grow.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed an honour to participate in this debate and perhaps to conclude it, but I must say that I am tired of the negativism displayed by hon. members opposite during this debate, and particularly by members of the Conservative party. I cannot understand this negativism because we in Canada have so many positive things going for us, in sharp contrast to the pronouncements made so far by hon. members opposite.
We have in Canada an immense geography, a land mass several times the size of Europe. We have a climate for every taste. We have people of 100 different origins. We can hear over 30 different languages spoken in our cities. We can speak to the whole world through international agencies in English or in French. After three years in Canada we can see an immigrant become a Canadian citizen. We have immense national resources. We have unity as our national goal, and we have multiculturalism as our dream.
We are known as peacekeepers in the world. We are respected at the United Nations. We are helpful to developing nations through the Canadian International Development Agency and through the International Development Research Centre. We are playing a major role in forging a new Law of the Sea at the United Nations, in concluding north-south negotiations in Paris, and in the disarmament talks and negotiations in New York.
We have in this country the auto pact, the Canada Development Corporation, the enterprise development program, Petro-Canada, Panarctic and the Anti-Inflation Board. We have the new horizons program, Canada Works and Young Canada Works. We have medicare, the family allowance program, hospital insurance, unemployment insurance, old age security, and the Canada Pension Plan.
We have in this country a modern agriculture, high quality production of food, a public transportation system among the best in the world. We have Air Canada, Canadian National, and the Canadian Wheat Board. We have the Maple Leaf. We had Expo. We have Sports Canada. We had the Olympic Games. We have yearly the Calgary Stampede. We have Team Canada. We have the experimental renewable energy project known as "The Arc" in Prince Edward Island. We have in Toronto the harbour front and the very fine city hall.

We have Northrop Frye, Marshall McLuhan, and Margaret Atwood. We have Pauline McGibbon, Claude Ryan, and Keith Spicer. We have Dr. Banting, Dr. Penfield, and Dr. Bethune. Hear, hear!

No wonder, then, that hundreds of thousands of people are asking to be admitted as immigrants into this country each year. No wonder that capital is flowing into Canada from all parts of the world because we are the envy of the whole world.
Against this background we have a negative, destructive, demoralizing, picayune and weak official opposition. We have a weak opposition as exemplified by the official financial critic of the Conservative party. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) was inaccurate, muddled and incompetent. He was off hundreds of millions of dollars in his critique in the budget of last year. Amongst others I did my part in exposing his blunders at that time. This time he stayed away from figures, but he could not resist giving us his old chesnut of indexing capital gains to help Canada's poor people. Needless to say, the proposal by the hon. member for York-Simcoe would be quite unworkable. It would permit someone to purchase an asset in December of one year and sell it in January of the succeeding year and claim a capital loss equal to the year over year change in the deflation factor. For an arch enemy of loopholes, the hon. member for York-Simcoe did pretty well here. Then he came forward with another dandy. That was the corporate tax credit to allow for the effects of inflation. Here you have the great champion in the fight against red tape suggesting that companies keep not just one but two sets of books to simplify matters, I suppose. If he should fail in his efforts in convincing the government to have this technique adopted, he may still look forward to having the satisfaction of becoming the honorary president of the Chartered Accountants Association of Canada.
The Financial Times of April 11 brought bad news for the hon. member for York-Simcoe. It reported just a week ago that $875 million in new investment for projects in Ontario and Alberta will be spent by United States companies this year, compared with $623 million two years ago. The commerce department in the United States reported that United States owned firms in Canada will push up total outlays by 16 per cent in 1977, and spending by manufacturing industries will climb by 27 per cent on their part. This is probably bad news for someone who has been crying about lack of confidence in our economy, as the member for York-Simcoe has

been doing for some time. Well, the Tories were in much better shape when their financial critic was the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies). Give us back the hon. member for Don Valley any time as a financial critic. We will welcome him. At least in 1973 he fought for wage and price controls.
I would be remiss if I did not devote a few moments to our housing records. I shall give the record of this Liberal government in reply to the New Democratic Party amendment which was written, perhaps, after reading an article written in the Toronto Star. The record is as follows: for low income housing for families and senior citizens our total output in 1976 was 20,900 units. In 1977 it is expected to go up to 21,890 units. Public housing in 1977 will substantially exceed the five-year average of 15,000 units per year. Funding for non-profit and co-operative housing went up from $328 million in 1976 to $351 million in 1977. This is quite a dramatic increase from the figure in 1972 when it was $43 million. Increased funds have been allocated to the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. During 1976 there were 15,550 homes for people with incomes averaging between $6,000 and $7,000 a year which benefited. In 1977 federal funds will upgrade some 22,300 dwelling units. These efforts to provide shelter for low income Canadians will mean some $924 million, or 67 per cent of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation's capital budget for 1977 alone.
To sum up in reply to the criticism on the part of the NDP, the direct low and middle income assistance provided by Ottawa, with the help of the taxpayers of Canada, was $1,177 million in 1976 and it is expected to be $1,374 million in 1977. 1 ask you whether this is a performance that deserves the criticism that the NDP expressed with respect to our government?
A debate like this would not be complete without speaking about unemployment and employment. We do have today in Canada 9,350,000 people working, and we have 944,000 Canadians out of work. That is a serious situation. It is good to put it into perspective because it is important to know that our economy is not stagnating but is in a position to create new jobs every year. This is what seems to be failing to catch the attention of opposition speakers.
In 1976 between the public and the private sectors in this country we had 209,000 jobs created. In 1975 there were
178.000	jobs created. In 1974 there were 383,000 jobs created. In 1973 there were 439,000 jobs created. In 1972 there were
256.000	jobs created. This indicates that from year to year, while we seem to have difficulties in absorbing the number of people who enter the labour market, we do achieve at the same time the creation of additional new jobs and therefore an increase in the total number of Canadians who have a job and who are employed.
If we look at the unemployment scene which is affecting our young people in a particular way these days, we do have to observe the fact that we have manpower shortages as well in certain occupations for which our educational system does not seem to be able to deliver trained people. In the January edition of the short term forecast of manpower called "For-
April 21, 1977

ward Occupational Imbalance Listing" published by the Department of Manpower and Immigration, we find a certain number of occupations for which there are shortages of people who are qualified and trained to fill these vacancies. These are jobs that do not require higher education. We do not seem to be able to produce, through our educational system, young people willing to do these jobs; but we do have demand for stationary engineers, pipe fitters and plumbers.
In some areas of Canada we need carpenters, diesel mechanics, millwrights, auto mechanics, machinists, upholsterers and the like. It seems that we would have to look at our entire educational system and our entire set of values in the late seventies to determine whether we will be able, through our educational system, to meet the demands of our labour market in the years to come.
However, let us look at the record for a moment because in my riding people have stopped me and asked why the government is putting only $100 million into job creation this year. We know that the figure of $100 million for job creation is the figure announced in the budget, but it has to be added to the $358 million which is going to be invested throughout the country to create jobs through the various programs sponsored under Canada Manpower, and that brings us to the figure of $458 million.
Let us look for a moment at manpower training in 1977. This government will be making available, through Manpower training services to unemployed Canadians, something like $583 million which, added to the amount made available for job creation, brings us pretty close to $1 billion. That is the real figure which ought to be emphasized when discussing the government's policy on job creation and job training.
With regard to youth unemployment and employment I would like to put on the record some figures which I think are quite worth while to meditate upon. These figures are not seasonally adjusted. In March of this year there were 2.256 million employed young Canadians below the age of 25, and
419,000	unemployed. In 1975 we were able to employ some 2.41 million young Canadians below the age of 25, while during that period there were 331,000 unemployed. In 1976 the situation was that 2.429 million Canadians below the age of 25 were employed and 355,000 were unemployed.
There has been an increase in the number of young Canadians unemployed over the past number of years. This is a matter of deep concern to all hon. members on all sides of the House and, of course, to the government. The question we have to ask is where the jobs are to come from? If we were to believe the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr Rodriguez), we would have the impression that 90 per cent of the jobs in Canada come from the public sector. We all know that that is not a fact. Actually the reverse is true, and 90 per cent of the jobs in Canada come from the private sector. Therefore, we have to ask ourselves how to generate the jobs that are needed to absorb the people entering the labour force and the unemployed.
The Budget-Mr. Caccia
In this budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) was not seeking publicity or cheap popularity but was saying that we should provide the incentives which are needed for the private sector to produce jobs in the long run, even though it might take several months before the machines get going again, while in the meantime the private sector in this country and around the world is still slowly trying to recover from the shock of inflation and the expenditures which have been generated through that wave of inflation we have experienced. However, that is too subtle and too difficult for the hon. member to understand, because if we were to do what he is proposing, we would have to buy up the entire private sector. We would have to generate jobs through job creation schemes in the public sector, and let the private sector just wait and see and fend for itself.
It is true that this may be an opportunity that this government is offering to the private sector in the hope that it will be a challenge which will be taken. Perhaps it is the most important one this government has ever offered to the private sector in the history of this country. In the months and years to come we will see whether this challenge will be accepted.
Another feature of this budget I find extremely encouraging is that for the first time we see regional incentives offered to help areas with high unemployment and with lagging economies. This is a great refining of budget making and of fiscal policies which should also be expanded to other measures in the future, perhaps like special tax rates and other fiscal incentives at the provincial level as well so that these will be joint federal and provincial policies to get the economies of the DREE designated areas in Canada going once and for all. The refinement of regional incentives is a very encouraging and welcome feature of this budget.
Hear, hear!

I am not a great believer in tax cuts because I do not know how such money is spent, and if it is not spent, which I suspect is the case, I do not know how it is saved and with whom it is saved. Instead of tax cuts-because the government needs revenues-I would rather see tax credits in areas of national concern; for instance in areas where we should be saving energy. Perhaps there should be tax credits for Canadians who carry out insulation projects on their own homes, and tax credits for the installation of solar and wind devices in Canadian homes. However, we will probably have to wait for these measures in our next budget.
In conclusion I would like to express a few words of support for the Anti-Inflation Board. Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the Webster dictionary defines "budget" as "a plan for the co-ordination of resources and expenditures," I suggest that what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) tabled in the House on March 31 could in no way be considered a budget. It might be called economic roulette, but in roulette there are remote odds that you can win. In this so-called budget nobody is going to win.
To realize what a guessing game this budget presentation has become and to see how wide of the mark the minister can be, one has only to look back to the budget which was tabled on May 25, 1976, a mere 11 months ago. His guess then was that the cash needs of the government in 1978 would show a significant decline, but in actual fact they have grown. The magnitude of error in the minister's estimates raises grave doubts about the competence of the forecaster and the government which gave him this responsibility.
Rarely, if ever, has the forecasting of the fiscal position of the federal government been as inaccurate as it was in that May budget, so it is understandable that this newest of prophecies has been received with utmost skepticism by the Canadian people. This co-ordination of resources and expenditures recommends that Canada be drawn even more heavily into debt.
The deficit planned for fiscal 1978 has reached an all-time high. In the six years ending last October federal spending jumped by 151 per cent There has been so much over-spending by the government in recent years that perpetually increasing deficits are required just to maintain a neutral fiscal policy stance.
No doubt the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has had time to reconsider, and to regret his ill-conceived opinion of the reason for the unfavourable economic climate which we are enduring today. In his questionable judgment the main reason for our expanding inflation is that Canadians are living beyond their means. It would be more accurate to assume that the government is living beyond the means of the Canadian people. With every level of the government taking large bites out of the incomes of Canadians, people are wondering if they can afford the present government.
During the past 15 years the 32 different kinds of Canadian taxes, direct and indirect, have risen 40 per cent. However, when the increases in incomes and prices over that period are calculated, the average family actually paid 239 per cent more tax in 1975 than in 1961. More of a family's income has had to go for taxes than was spent on food, clothing and shelter combined.
Increased taxation means expanding government control at all levels, and especially at the federal level. It is well on the way to controlling us out of an independent way of life. With these extra millions and millions of dollars going into the government coffers, there needs to be some explanation of our ever-accelerating rate of national debt.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I regret having to interrupt the hon. member, but it being 9.45 o'clock, it is my duty at this time pursuant to section 8 of Standing Order 60 to interrupt the proceedings and put forthwith the question on the motion now before the House. All those in favour of the motion will please say yea.
Yea.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: All those opposed will please say nay.

Nay.
The government has been so preoccupied with the redistribution of wealth in Canada that it has forgotten how to produce that wealth competitively, and we can no longer pretend that we are a prosperous nation.
We have become the country with the highest cost production. Canadian manufacturers are now at a competitive disadvantage, and this in a country where it is essential to remain competitive and to hold our position as a trading nation.
During the 1960's there was an annual trade deficit in manufactured products of about $3 billion. This deficit has been growing ever larger and last year it topped the $10 billion mark.
Until a few years ago we were content to let our exports of natural resources offset the growing deficit in manufactured products. Now we must face up to the fact that those natural resources are not infinite and that our deterioration of efficiency in the marketplace has to be stemmed and reversed. There must be an environment created which will allow the manufacturing sector to realize its potential and make a meaningful contribution to the economic future of all Canadians.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In my opinion the yeas have it.
And more than five members having risen:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Call in the members.

speechtext:
